speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Terrorists are returning from Syria and Iraq to Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They could return to terrorist leanings after their release.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Reports have shown that the Marawi conflict has generated potential terrorists, adding to the regional threat we face.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In fact, every single inhabitable continent in our world has suffered a terror attack since the beginning of this year alone, 2017.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In Fort Lauderdale, Florida, a man shot and killed five people at the airport.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Just last night, we heard news of a possible terror attack in Las Vegas, 59 people tragically killed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In Manchester, an explosion killed 22 children, youths and adults at an Ariana Grande concert.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Again, just over the weekend, in Marseille, France, two women were stabbed to death.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In Jakarta, two explosions at a busy bus station killed three police officers and injured 10 people.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In Melbourne, a woman was taken hostage, two men were shot, and three police officers injured in the line of duty in June of this year.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In Colombia, South America, an explosion at a shopping centre killed three women and injured 11 others.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And in Mali, West Africa, five people were shot at a tourist resort in June.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, should we move on the assumption that an attack will never happen to us?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The Straits Times reported that there was an Arabic publication circulated last October that identified two entities here, the Singapore Exchange and a port, as targets as part of a wider bid to damage American and Western interests.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In a separate report by the Jakarta-based Institute for Policy Analysis of Conflict, those heading the Marawi network had urged militants on Telegram to attack targets in Singapore, Thailand and Japan.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: According to a report on "Risk and Resilience" for the Department of Homeland Security in United States (US), pre-event activity is key to resilience.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It places importance on the capacity to anticipate, plan and prepare to cope with threats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: An important aspect of this pre-event activity is being vigilant.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In London, recent attacks involved vans being driven on pedestrian walkways and knife attacks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It happened in very public areas, accessible to pedestrians and vehicles.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Low cost, highly visible, possibility for lone-wolf operations, vulnerable targets, are dangerous concoctions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Without concrete bollards on every crowded street, checks on every bag carried on the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT), restriction on the sales of all kinds of knives ─ even kitchen knives ─ this would be near impossible.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Minister K Shanmugam has said, "You can't turn the entire city into a garrison." No matter what interventions the state puts in to try to prevent a terrorist attack, it is very likely that the first responders will be the citizens on the ground.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Therefore, it is not just for the specialist forces or the Police to be alert to such threats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The possibility of a terror attack needs to be ingrained in the consciousness of everyone.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It should not cripple us in Singapore with fear.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Rather, that consciousness should help us to know how to spot suspicious activities and how to react to them in a calm and systematic fashion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The signs of suspicious persons, articles and vehicles have been disseminated through the SGSecure App and other means.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But knowing the signs is not enough; we need to instil the culture of vigilance that will cause people to look up, observe their surroundings and know how to make a judgement call.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That judgement call includes following instructions in the SGSecure App, which are "Run, Hide, Tell".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How well we are able to respond to the terror attack would very much depend on how we, the first responders, cooperate with the Police by giving information through the SGSecure app.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Hence, according to the SGsecure guide, we should TELL.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: T for the total number of attackers, E for equipment or weapons being carried, L for look of attackers, and L for location of attackers ─ where they are now and moving towards.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Our response as citizens will be crucial in order for the response from our uniformed staff to be even more effective.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It could be a vehicle marauding through the crowd on a footway, or a knife-wielding group of men in a crowded restaurant.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is our duty as citizens of Singapore to help report suspicious activity before the threat materialises.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: If the threat is so well-disguised and an attack does occur, then we should provide as accurate information as we can through the SGSecure app.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To be truly secure, all of us − very Singaporean − has a part to play to be vigilant.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is also important that Singaporeans work synergistically with the uniformed forces in the face of a terror attack.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Equally, the uniformed services − Home Team and SAF − will need to work synergistically with each other.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Singapore is increasing exercises and trainings between the Home Team and SAF as well as between the Home Team and the citizenry, through local Emergency Preparedness days.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But a look at how other countries are planning their responses to terror attacks may be useful for Singapore's policymakers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: For example, in Hong Kong, the Standing Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear Planning Group meets regularly to formulate contingency plans and procedures for threatened or possible attacks, including terror attacks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is made up of specialists from various departments and agencies, such as the hospitals, laboratories, police force, civil aid service and fire service.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is a multidisciplinary team on call, 24 hours a day, to assess threats and give advice on the spot.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In Australia, the Prime Minister Malcom Turnbull wanted personnel from the defence force to be placed within law enforcement agencies to assist in coordination efforts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We could study the Hong Kong and Australia models to assess what best practices we could import into Singapore's anti-terror regime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Another key strategy to secure resilience against the psychology of fear that terrorists seek to sow is to promote unity in the aftermath of a terror attack.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How we respond to a terror attack is important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A response using Home Team and SAF military hardware is key but let us also realise that Singapore and Singaporeans must win the psychological battle.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Our unity will ensure we are victorious over any ill the attacks seek to incite.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: According to SAFE-COMMS which was commissioned by the European Union, a key message should be, "We will not allow terrorists to spread fear and horror and gain the upper hand." The next message is, "We know what we are doing", then the next message is, "All those affected will receive all the support that they need." The basic principles are rapid restoration of confidence and security, transparent trust-building information policy, calmly competent yet sensitive treatment of all those that are directly and indirectly involved, leadership with integrity and credibility, and decisive action.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The message of social connectedness and hope is important, especially in the aftermath of an attack.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In December 2014, a lone gunman held 17 hostages at a cafe in Sydney for more than 16 hours.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Within a few hours of the attack, a hashtag campaign entitled "I'll Ride With You" went viral on the Internet.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Australians stood together with their Muslim brothers and sisters.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The point is, we need to win the psychological value.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is not just the day itself, but the day after the attack.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We do not point our fingers but hold hands and stand united together against terror.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But to do so, we need to prepare now.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A first step now could be to prepare posters and other paraphernalia to send such messages quickly and visibly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These are some of what the residents in the constituency I serve, Ulu Pandan, organised in terms of banners.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They have been printed, they are in the Community Centre, ready to be put up at locations throughout the constituency should there be an attack. "We are one people, one nation, one Singapore", "Deny terrorism a victory, let's stay united".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The four hands of our races ─ Singaporean Chinese, Malay, Indian and Eurasians ─ protecting our precious Singapore, holding it together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Red and white chosen ─ the colours of our flag. "No to disunity", "Terrorism will not win".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These messages displayed the day-after are what Singaporeans can see and will stir them to say, "Yes, we are in this together", "Yes, it will be okay." So, first, we need to promote vigilance and resilience amongst Singaporeans to deter and overcome terrorist attacks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And that was the first part of the Motion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To take the appropriate action, we have a range of laws that may be applied.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We only need to look to the recent terror attack on London Bridge in Borough Market to see why muscular laws which gives police proactive and pre-emptive powers are important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The Independent reported that Scotland Yard acknowledged that the ringleader of the terrorist who carried out the London Bridge attack was known to the police and MI5 for extremism before he went on his rampage of murder and maiming.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The British Broadcasting Corporation reported that the ringleader had previously appeared in a Channel 4 documentary about the presence of violent extremists in British cities.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In Singapore, the laws must not work to hinder investigation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: When pre-emptive detention is necessary, we must act and administer it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We cannot have our hands tied behind our backs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: More so, in light of what the Minister for Home Affairs shared just three weeks ago.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The rate of being influenced has decreased from 22 months, not to 20 months, not to 12 months, but to two months.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Our laws in Singapore must facilitate early action, pre-emptive action, to reduce the possibility of terror threats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Our laws do help deter the spread of radicalised teachings, which promote violent extremism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And with the changing nature of terrorist attacks in the world, the shorter period for radicalisation, we may need to review our laws to ensure that they are flexible enough, that they are robust enough, to mitigate against and ameliorate the morphing nature of terror attacks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Allow me, Mr Speaker, to go through the Acts and, by so doing, hopefully get across to those who wish to do us harm that we have the requisite laws to act pre-emptively and swiftly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: A different raft of laws targets the action of spreading violent extremism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These can be found in the Penal Code and the Sedition Act.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Seditious tendency is defined to include "promot  hostility between different races or classes of the population of Singapore." When the need arises, there is the Internal Security Act (ISA).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: For instance, section 20 empowers the Minister to prohibit or set conditions regarding the possession of documents that contain any incitement to violence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But, to add real value, the laws should also aim to assist the detained and help rehabilitate them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Rehabilitation and reintegration are important strategies to stem the spread of such violent extremism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This makes crucial the work of organisations, such as the Religious Rehabilitation Group (RRG).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Its mission statement expands on the importance of rehabilitation to the detainee: "Rehabilitation seeks to counter detainees' ideological misunderstanding of religion and help them come to terms with the fact that they have been misled." It was reported that the restriction order of one of the former members of Jemaah Islamiyah (JI) was allowed to lapse; he is no longer required for further supervision under the restriction order regime.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Therefore, we have an arsenal of laws to empower pre-emptive action, preventive detention, leading to rehabilitation and, hopefully, reintegration.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But laws alone cannot offer Singapore's complete counter-offence to terrorism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Terrorism is not the problem of a single race.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is not the problem of a single religion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In 2011, he committed Norway's worst attack and was convicted of mass murder and terrorism offences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: At that time, it was the world's deadliest terror attack by a lone gunman.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Many of his victims were teenagers on a recent summer retreat.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Besides the shooting rampage on the island of Utoya, he planted a bomb in a van in Oslo's city centre.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: He was a self-declared fascist, who held strong anti-Muslim sentiments.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What he did was detestable, horrid and inhuman.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: There can be no room for violent extremism in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Therefore, acts of violence, such as those acts towards all vulnerable communities in the Rakhine state, should stop.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To see children suffer like that grates against humanity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In the case of terror attacks around the world, people of different races and religions have shown through their actions and courage that they will not condone violence and the killing of the innocent.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In July this year, Channel 4 News ran a documentary on a group of Christians in Mosul who were rescuing Muslims from the fire of the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) snipers there.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They risked their lives to save innocent Muslim people.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It was reported by Channel NewsAsia on 5 August that during the fighting in Marawi, a Muslim villager chose to stay put in his house and put his own life in danger, even when his friends and relatives begged him to vacate it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Because he had people he was protecting there.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They had run out of food and he helped them escape from the militants' rampage.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Terrorism is an affront to all of us, regardless of race or religion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And so, we can and need to have a collective counter-offence to it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: By continuing to strengthen multiracialism and social cohesion in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We need to view our multiracialism as an asset, a muscular asset.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Different ethnic communities define their identity in different ways which may change over time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Multiracialism does not mean we give up our ethnic identity which is informed by race, our culture and upbringing and, to an extent, by our religious beliefs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is not about everybody becoming the same.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Multiracialism is about appreciating diversity − diversity in race, language, religious beliefs and, at the same time, being loyal to our duty we have as Singaporeans, that is, the duty to advance Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In fact, multiracialism makes Singapore a multiskilled, multitalented and multifaceted country.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Within Singapore, our population can lean on the different skills, thought processes, talents and languages of the people from the different races who live in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: When foreign governments visit Singapore, explore trading opportunities and collaboration, our multiracialism becomes an immediate asset.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Foreign governments, trading partners and tourists can relate to the cultures within Singapore which may be present in their own home countries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Internationally, when Singapore Government leaders and businessmen visit China, Indonesia, Malaysia, India and many other countries, we are able to connect with them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Because cultures are understood well and sometimes shared.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We offer those whom we visit and with whom we trade a multiracial Singapore − multicultured, multiskilled, multitalented.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: For me, multiracialism is not an academic issue.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Singaporean Eurasians are multiracial in our very genetic makeup and believe in Singapore's multiracialism to the core.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We do not want to discard the English, Portuguese, Dutch, Burmese and the Indian influence in us but, at the same time, we have a duty to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We are multiracial in the very core of our identity but, at the same time, profess fierce loyalty to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Over the centuries, in terms of ethnicity, we have become an amalgamation of many races, including Dutch, English, Portuguese, Ceylonese and Burmese.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: One cannot divide us and put a bit of us back into the different countries our ancestors came from.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Our duty is to Singapore and her future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, being part of the Eurasian race, I can understand what it means to be culturally aware of ethnic heritage and all the richness it offers but, at the same time, being completely focused on being Singaporeans first and foremost.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I hope we will all aspire towards retaining cultural identities coupled with a strong duty to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It seeks to disunite communities, make us point fingers at one another, become factious.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But with a cohesive spirit and multiracialism, we can defeat the ills terrorism seeks to sow.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That multiracialism is a strength can be illustrated in tangible ways.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Rather, what mattered to them was the RACE Singapore had to win.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What mattered was the mission − advancing Singapore's flag on the track.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Growing up, when I was playing lots of hockey, I had Chinese, Indian, Malay, Punjabi, Eurasian teammates.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: When we played against teams from other countries, our teams used to communicate on the pitch in different languages − Malay, English, Mandarin, Punjabi, Tamil, Hokkien.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Sometimes, using very colourful verbs and nouns, best not repeated, especially here.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The other teams were confused at hearing this collage of languages.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We used our multiracialism and multilingual ability as assets.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What mattered most to us was whether Singapore was up against the opponent on the scoreboard.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Singapore has been recognised as a multicultural society and that has also been independently recognised as a strength.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In an article in September 2017 in the Asian Tribune, the author cited the Singapore Government as having recognised "the importance of maintaining and fostering racial harmony" and that it had implemented policies and safeguards to that end.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Left to itself, people tend to gravitate along racial lines.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: When there is an unfamiliarity among ethnic groups, lack of social cohesion exists.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The unfortunate consequence is a sense of distrust among the races.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We have had to work hard at it and we need to continue to work hard at it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is an aspiration, an ideal that we strive and need to continue to strive towards.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, what have we done to move towards our aspirations?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: People of a different race, of a different religion, live next to one another.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: There is some familiarity, a platform for social integration through interaction, transcending ethnic boundaries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Another important pillar is the Inter-Racial and Religious Confidence Circles (IRCCs).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: They bring leaders of the different religious, ethnic and community groups together to build friendship and trust.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Their good work had brought all of us of different races and religions together and has greatly contributed to furthering our ideal of multiracialism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This picture was taken at the reappointment ceremony of our constituency's IRCC this year.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: All of us, the races, Chinese, Malay, Indian and Eurasian, and many religions were present and represented at that table, cutting a cake together, symbolising the re-appointment of the IRCC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That was a very meaningful ceremony, possibly only in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: I think all of us do ceremonies in each of our constituencies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What I mean by "only in Singapore" is that this type of ceremony happens only in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: It is an affront to Singapore and her values.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That way, we secure for ourselves a happy irony.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The threat of terrorism and the risk of radicalisation and extremism cannot be underestimated nor taken for granted.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With advancements in technologies and increasing global connectivity, terrorist and separatist cells are emboldened and have more convenient platforms to recruit similar-minded individuals to fight their cause, no matter how insidious that cause may be, usually made under the guise of seemingly religious or cultural grounds.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, fighting terrorism goes beyond legislative enactments and enforcement.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some may think the onus and responsibility of looking out for such threats lie within the individual or those closest to the individual.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, just as fighting crime and ensuring public safety is a shared responsibility which requires a common effort and resolve, so is the threat of terrorism and the risk of radicalisation and extremism.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And this upstream work cannot just be the effort of asatizahs or Islamic religious scholars and teachers alone.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, there is a need to work across religions, races, cultures and even languages in tackling these threats upstream.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, I would propose involving as many first points of contact as possible, be it through our grassroots movement, Family Service Centres, Social Service Offices, non-government organisations (NGOs) and voluntary welfare organisations.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Volunteers and officers in such organisations are in frequent and direct contact with Singaporeans on a daily basis.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They ought to be trained to pick up tell-tale signs or potential problems which may escalate into situations of an individual being radicalised or, worse, committing acts of terrorism, be it religiously motivated or otherwise.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some tell-tale signs could include being reclusive or withdrawn, spending too much time online, developing sudden changes in views or perceptions or behaviour, or developing intense frustrations or having anger management issues.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Upon the detection of such worrying tell-tale signs, these first points of contact should make referrals to the RRG or other certified counsellors for further assistance and follow-up.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The call has always been for families and friends to look out for such tell-tale signs, but families and friends may not always be impartial or neutral enough or may not always be quick enough to inform the relevant authorities for follow-up help.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, we would need many other first points of contact to manage this better.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, I would urge the Government to support initiatives where some of our youths are trained to be youth ambassadors and youth leaders, to mitigate the threat of radicalisation and extremist ideologies through youth activism.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our youth ambassadors or leaders are the ones to lead our youths on meaningful engagements and socially constructive projects that build communities and not partake in missions or causes that tear down communities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are also the ones who are trained to pick up tell-tale signs of the possible threat of radicalisation and extremist ideologies among their fellow youths, before these evolve into acts of terrorism.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, there is also a need to seek the involvement of significant others in promoting vigilance against and mitigating the threat of radicalisation and extremism among our youths.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: An important group of significant others is made up of our teachers, in both our mainstream and secular, as well as religious, educational institutions.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just as some teachers are trained as psychological counsellors in many of our mainstream schools, we would also need teachers to be trained as first points of contact to identify students or youths who are being radicalised or may be at risk of developing extremist ideologies or being involved in acts of terrorism.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These teachers would work closely with the RRG, the Ministry of Home Affairs or other Government agencies that would be able to follow up with these students or youths, such as getting in touch with their parents or families, counselling them, enrolling them in rehabilitative programmes, or getting them involved in meaningful and socially constructive activities to redirect their ideas, energies and focus.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At this point, Mr Speaker, Sir, please allow me to continue in Malay.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   The involvement of educators and religious teachers in countering the threat of radicalism, extremism and terrorism amongst our youths is very important and necessary.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just as how some teachers from mainstream schools are trained to become counsellors to help students who may be stressed or have personal problems, we also need religious teachers in our madrasahs who are trained to help our students and youths who may be at risk of being radicalised.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These religious teachers can refer such students or youths to the right persons for further assistance.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, we should also encourage our religious teachers to be more active in sharing their knowledge and views about the context of multiracial and multi-religious life in Singapore with our youths, especially through the social media platforms.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We do have religious teachers who are active in social media in order to engage our youths, like Ustaz Mizi Wahid and Ustaz Irwan Hadi.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I hope that the number of such social media-savvy religious teachers will increase.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They have the potential to become positive influencers who can shape the views and perceptions of our youths.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also hope that our Islamic College will become a symbol of Islamic education and scholarship that is excellent, progressive and inclusive, and able to become a renowned global Islamic institution.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to touch on the third item of this Motion, that is, investment in our pillars of multiracialism and multi-religious life, to defeat the threat of radicalism and terrorism.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should continue our efforts to uphold multiracialism and multi-religious life in Singapore, not only to achieve racial harmony, but also in our efforts to counter the threat of radicalism, extremism and terrorism.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These efforts should continue at all levels and by every person, and not only by the Government or religious teachers and educators.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, please allow me to continue in English.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Each individual plays an important role in our efforts against the threats of radicalism, extremism and terrorism.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, there is another endeavour that we need to partake in, that of ensuring that we do not swing to the other extreme of allowing any form of stereotypes or deep-seated biases to develop against any particular race or religion.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What we have nurtured here in Singapore − inclusivity and trust based on multiracialism and multiculturalism − are very precious.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must continue to work and do good together, and we need to continue to be sensitised to the needs of others, especially the minorities among us.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And here, when I speak of the minorities, I am not just referring to those of race and religion alone; I am also referring to those of abilities and which happen as a result of social constructs, be it cognitive, communicative and so on.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we progress as a nation, let us strengthen the bonds that exist among us, continue to be inclusive and magnanimous, and make sure we do not leave anyone behind, stranded or paralysed because of their race, religion or abilities. "The beauty of the world lies in the diversity of its people".

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us continue to uphold multiracialism, multiculturalism and inclusivity, for it gives us fortitude as a people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The spectre of terrorism has been with us for slightly over 15 years since the bombing of the Twin Towers on 11 September 2001.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many of us remember the shocking revelations of Al-Qaeda-inspired plans to attack foreign embassies and commercial establishments in Singapore with truck bombs, and the arrests of some members of the JI terrorist organisation in Singapore shortly thereafter.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More than 15 years later, Singaporeans may be surprised to know that, even up to today, there is no internationally agreed upon definition for terrorism.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One reason for this is the objection of groups and communities fighting for nationalist or separatist causes as a result of being disenfranchised or excluded by the state.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such atrocities are fertile ground for terrorism, and some acts of terror undertaken by oppressed people do not lend themselves to simple understanding or even condemnation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At times, the reality of any multiracial country hosting different communities, races and religions, including Singapore, is that atrocities in lands far away from ours will affect our people and pull at our heartstrings and our identities, too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This prospect has taken on a whole new dimension with the advent of social media.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even though we are one people as Singaporean citizens, many of us host other identities and even biases, alongside our status as Singaporeans, regardless if we are a minority community or in the majority.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the 1980s, the ISD stepped in to prevent the Singapore Sikh community from taking their support through Sikh religious institutions for an independent Sikh homeland in Punjab too far.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Most historically, in the war years, many Chinese in Malaya contributed and supported the resistance against the Japanese Imperial Forces through China and in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Muslims are deeply affected when innocent Palestinians die in reprisal killings carried out by the Israeli state.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While all these examples are not directly comparable, the point is that no matter what our race or religion, many of us do feel a deep sense of outrage when our kinsmen or women are bullied or wantonly killed anywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But add religion to the mix, and feelings can cut to the bone.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a multiracial nation, we are susceptible to this reality of contested identities and even more so now, as our population grows in size and newer Singaporeans join our ranks.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, whether we are Singaporeans by birth or by choice, we are all invested in the well-being of this country, in all aspects.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We have to acknowledge that we pay allegiance to the President, our flag and to the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, a Constitution that makes it the duty of any government to look after the interests of racial and religious minorities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And so long as we do, our first loyalty is to Singapore and our way of life, which includes the well-being of families and friends regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This must be so, and we must never relegate this first loyalty under any circumstances.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, I have observed ordinary Singaporeans, local NGOs and institutions, and even the Prime Minister in some cases, being openly supportive of humanitarian initiatives in some of the most politically tense and fraught regions of the world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a Singaporean, I identified with the call of the Buddhist community and it made me proud to be a Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And it is this common humanity that we will have to call upon to deal with the type of terrorism we see today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, a successful ISIS terrorist strike in Singapore falsely carried out in the name of Islam will test our social cohesion and resilience as one people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Malay/Muslim community will come under the spotlight.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some extremist Muslims, particularly those overseas, may even celebrate such an attack, seeding more doubt against the entire Malay/Muslim community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The ubiquitous nature of the social media will see some viral commentary which may prove hard to ignore, affecting the morale of the country and precipitating senseless reprisals, not all of which may be physical acts of violence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Avoiding the Malay/Muslim community and the desire not to have anything to do with them are equally, if not, more damaging, because turning on the Malay/Muslim community is the magic pill ISIS seeks to legitimise their narrative, one of oppression against Muslims.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A few days ago, as the Workers' Party Members were discussing this Motion, Mr Low Thia Khiang recalled conversations with his constituents and friends of some Chinese Singaporeans being shielded from violence by their Malay friends and neighbours who invited them to stay in their homes with family members during the racial riots in the 1960s.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We will have to harness such examples of our common humanity to get on with our lives in the advent of a terrorist attack in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such stories serve an important unifying purpose, as is the pursuit of knowledge on matters pertaining to faith in the context of a multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I do appreciate that not all stories are comfortable to discuss, but they do need to be shared because a sense of perspective, even if it is the Government's perspective, can be critical.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some years ago, but less so now, in the course of house visits, I hear allegations about the Government discriminating against the Malay community in the banning of the call to prayer or azan over loud hailers, a policy introduced many years ago.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When I share that some of our Chinese friends occasionally raise concerns about the Government reserving land for Chinese temples within industrial estates, unlike mosques, which tend to be centrally-located within our communities and with good transport links, the conversations suddenly take on a very different complexion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Views which originally started out as outright discrimination by the Government start to moderate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When one hears the azan walking around Jalan Sultan today, one realises that there can be nuance to policy decisions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And there must always be scope for nuance in policy decisions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is one reality of living in a multiracial country, the inevitably uneven nature of give-and-take in matters of race and religion, a matter to which I will come back to shortly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Members of this House would agree that HDB living and urban living in general, with the races co-existing cheek by jowl does increase the prospects of interracial misunderstandings to take place.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They are usually innocuous, such as a shift worker trying to get some sleep or a student studying for exams, just as your Malay neighbours are hosting a marriage or your Chinese neighbours are carrying out funeral rites at the void deck or of your Indian neighbours pounding spices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just as often as we hear complaints in our HDB estates of open burning of joss paper and the illegal parking of vehicles by congregants of various faiths at temples, mosques or churches which spill over outside, we also hear of neighbours who are comfortable amongst one another and can rely on one another in times of need, exemplified in not just the food or greetings they share, but the willingness to be race-neutral, open-minded and communicative, traits which are vital to living in a multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: All Members of this House would have experienced this in the course of their grassroots work.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chauvinistic behaviour, an attitude of superiority, an intolerance exhibited by superiors or co-workers at the workplace where we spend a large part of our day-to-day lives, will permeate not just into our attitudes but into the values we pass on to our loved ones.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This damages the quality of our multiracialism and we must be mindful of passing on our prejudices and biases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the same breath, workers of any race must recognise that we all must strive to do our best, not just in words but in deeds.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A can-do spirit, a positive work ethic and a common sense of mission aligned with the needs of your company or organisation can actually play a pivotal role in teaching racists about the futility and irrelevance of holding on to racist attitudes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some Singaporeans might have to leave a job because of latent or even perceived discrimination, but whatever the bad experience, leave the prejudice or the racism you have experienced behind too, for not all five fingers are the same.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is a testimony to Singaporeans and the sort of people we have moulded ourselves to become over the last 50 years, that we have come to live in peace with one another in spite of the occasional hiccup, which is not unusual for a multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, I see our multiracialism not just as a constant work in progress, but a glass that is half full, as opposed to half empty.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On this note, I would like to acknowledge the real and optical comfort the presence of members of the Inter-Religious Organisation (IRO) have communicated to many Singaporeans when they appear at various events.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I marvelled at the boldness and imagination to create giant man-made trees in the middle of the city and to create a wonderful garden where plants of various species could be housed, tended to with great care to let them flourish.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I recall that when plans for the Gardens were first unveiled, I had thought how unreal it was.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But now, when I see the happy faces of families and visitors there, I have no doubt that the endeavour has paid off.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It occurred to me that what we have in Singapore is somewhat similar to our Gardens by the Bay.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With boldness and imagination, we had economically transformed Singapore and, with the ideals of a multiracial and multicultural society in mind, we created social policies to bring about equal opportunities for our citizens regardless of race, language or religion to flourish and co-exist peacefully together.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our diverse cultures are like the diverse exotic flowers at Gardens by the Bay.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is nothing preordained about our economic transformation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Land was reclaimed to build more housing and specialised industries, technology to recycle and desalinate water.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And we attracted investments to create jobs we otherwise did not have.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Similarly, there is nothing preordained about the social harmony among our citizens of different races and different religions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the incident in Charlottesville, US, and in the Rakhine province of Myanmar and in various suburbs in France show us so vividly, in countries where there are racially and religiously diverse populations, when interracial or interreligious issues are not handled well, there can be bloodshed and chaos in society.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Government has taken a practical and unbiased look at what drives communities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While nurturing each community, our Government is cognisant of what outcomes may naturally arise, given inherent preferences and motivations, and takes actions through social policies to ensure that the delicate balance among different communities is maintained and trust built.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Punggol recently, I welcomed three religious organisations to my constituency.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They each serve their congregants but they are close enough to one another for their congregants to see one another and to know one another if they make the effort to do so.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Would it have happened naturally if the Government had not put it into the town plans?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is natural for members of a community to want to group together.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But there could be downsides as communities can end up being segregated.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, while providing spaces for communities to practise their ways of life and religious worship, social policies have also been needed to create more common space through town planning in this case to bring communities closer together.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As individuals and as communities, we also can, through our own efforts, reach out to build bridges across communities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But we also need a system to support individual and community effort to nurture, guide and also protect.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In this example, town planning provided a conducive environment for congregants of different religions to get to know one another.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Grassroots organisations then proactively reached out to all three religious organisations to do good for the community together.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Does the Government's practical and realist approach make the policies any less aspirational?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Like our young, we all wish for a progressive and equal society.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But just wishing for it will not make it a reality.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Recognising human nature, natural tendencies, objectively distinguishing causes from outcomes, and then taking action, step by step, to strengthen and protect what has been created may bring us closer to realising the ideals our nation aspires to.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Recently, we have seen growing religious extremism in many countries around the world which heightens tensions and differences among communities.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Local grievances and regional conflicts provide a rallying cause, which charismatic preachers can leverage on.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Racial and religious fault lines are fertile ground for domestic political exploitation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such influences accentuate differences, create walls among different communities and isolate groups.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is it by looking at the social harmony we currently enjoy and assuming that all is well?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Or is it to continue investing in multiracialism so that it becomes the best socio-weapon against threats to the cohesion of our society?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have to be careful not to be lulled into just saying the pretty words by not wanting to point out realities which may be inconvenient.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Hokkien, they say, "Mai zou pai nang", that is, "do not be the bad person", and allude to higher aspirations of multiracialism while leaving the work to others to do, and offer no practical solutions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Because if we all do that, then, we may inadvertently dismantle what has brought us here and discourage those who have contributed and are still contributing to our social harmony.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Was it an ideology that the Minister Mentor had asked rhetorically in Parliament as recently as in 2009 over a debate on our founding tenets of multiracialism and multiculturalism?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: No, it is an aspiration, he remarked in return.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Will we achieve it, he asked again. "I do not know," the Minister Mentor said, "We have to keep on trying".

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have to, so that our people, regardless of race, language or religion, can flourish in our unique garden city where there is always sufficient nutrition for everyone.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Perhaps, individual care unique to their backgrounds, but always safe where no weeds can harm them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our garden will be more beautiful and a greater wonder to all through its diversity.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   Last month, I attended a very special event.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was proposed by the Punggol grassroots organisation, organised by the Al Islah Mosque, and attended by the local Catholic church and Buddhist temple.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They did charity work together by delivering daily necessities to the residents and giving blessings.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The theme of this event was "Blessing in Harmony".

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The decision to do this was jointly made by the three religious organisations, because they felt they shared a common cause.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I remember we came up to one flat with a cross hanging on its door.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We naturally turned to the Catholic priest who then went up to knock on the door.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She was Catholic but she can only speak dialect.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The priest, however, can only speak in English.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They made many gestures and tried to communicate but still failed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Luckily, there were people from the temple and the grassroots organisation who could speak dialects.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They stepped forward to help with the interpretation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Both the priest and the lady were very happy, and we were also very happy seeing that.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I think perhaps this scene can only be seen in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Here, the distance between the different religions and races can be very small.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although we are different, we can still support one another and be inclusive.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we can respect and accommodate one another.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew once said: "I do not expect the Government to assimilate everyone.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I will not even try because that would be a meaningless attempt. …However, I would say integration is possible.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our integration is based on shared values, attitudes, language and, ultimately, a common culture." We look forward to what Mr Lee had envisioned.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We know that religious and racial harmony does not come out of the blue.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Instead, it needs to be nurtured by our efforts, bit by bit.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Biologists say that living beings have a natural tendency to protect genes similar to themselves.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Human beings also have a natural tendency to prefer one's own race.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If this natural tendency is not developed properly, racial divide will occur, and racial divide is the beginning of ethnic confrontation and conflict.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The US has always been troubled by the race issue.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If we take a look at the deeper issue, we can see that the long-time separation between the whites and the blacks has sowed the seeds for racial confrontation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Ethnic issues in other parts of the world are roughly the same.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Separation creates misunderstanding, misunderstanding leads to confrontation, and confrontation leads to bloodshed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The solution is to bring the distance closer.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Singapore Government has been bringing the distance closer all these years.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another example is to implement English education but, at the same time, keeping the mother tongue.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This enables various races to communicate better and avoid misunderstanding and estrangement.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Racial harmony is not the work of the Government alone.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, we can all play a part.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As long as we can take a small step forward when dealing with Singaporeans of different races and religions, show respect and understanding, we will then generate positive energies.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Just like during the Al Islah event, people from the temple and the grassroots organisation take a small step forward to help people from other religions and races.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This one small step can change a lot.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Human beings also have another natural instinct, and that is love and tolerance.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Love and tolerance allow us to love and help one another beyond race, religion and border.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Love and tolerance are not just a slogan.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From the interreligious and interracial event which our local mosque has organised, we see love and tolerance.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore's Malay/Muslim organisations have been playing an important role in preventing extremism and promoting racial harmony.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Against the background that overseas terrorist organisations are spreading extremist thoughts, this initiative is very timely and will help guide local Muslims in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The step taken by the local Muslim community has prevented social divide and made the distance between people smaller.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In order to maintain Singapore's racial harmony, we must act and continue to improve our system, so that we can create a common space among different religions and races.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let us work hand in hand and do good together.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When everyone takes one small step forward, the distance between us will become smaller.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We will be more united, and we will be safer, too.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Racial harmony begins from each one of us.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A small step from one person will be a big step for the society towards social harmony.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, I support the Motion and would like to make some suggestions towards the effort to strengthen social cohesion so that Singaporeans of all races and religions can stand strong together, with one voice, and prevent, combat and defeat the scourge of radicalism and terrorism together.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It has frequently been reported that terror incidents taking place, either by certain groups or by individuals, were committed by those who have been influenced and lured by radical ideologies.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many experts who monitored and observed this situation have concluded that the scourge of terrorism and radicalism cannot be easily countered and stopped, and it is highly likely that this situation will persist in the future.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The question is, what makes a person become so influenced by radicalism until that person becomes so caught up in it and dares to commit acts of terror, killing innocent lives and destroying public property?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: How can someone's mind be able to accept that there is nothing wrong with committing acts of terror that are based on the justification of achieving change and justice?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This process is usually used by hardline extremists who submit to certain religious or political ideologies.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Hence, the best way to counter such radical elements is by inculcating authentic religious values, knowledge that strengthens one's character and also community and national values amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We have seen how JI and ISIS have misused Islamic teachings to manipulate and radicalise the minds of individuals and, hence, influencing them to turn towards violence and terrorism by claiming that this is meant to uphold truth and justice.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In Singapore, preventive and rehabilitative steps have been taken and implemented to counter religious ideologies that are radical or extremist in nature.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Local religious teachers and Islamic scholars have stepped forward, worked together and contributed their time and energy voluntarily to help rehabilitate individuals who were taken in by radical propaganda.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Both initiatives, the RRG and ARS, showed that it is important and necessary to have efforts that inculcate fundamental and authentic religious values to counter and prevent radicalism and extremism in religion.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Prevention is a very effective way to counter the scourge of radicalism.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Efforts for upstream intervention should be done by inculcating relevant knowledge to counter the wave of radicalism, a scourge that is haunting the global community.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because the scourge of terrorism, globally as well as in Singapore, has shown that religious doctrine has been used to radicalise individuals.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe that the inculcation of authentic religious teachings at a young age through the national education system is a more effective method in the effort to prevent radical religious thinking.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We should be open to make slight adjustments and changes if the situation calls for it, in order to guarantee social cohesion and the prosperity of the nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Earlier, I shared how extremists and terrorists manipulate minds in the effort to radicalise an individual.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Psychology is a field of science pertaining to the mind and behaviour.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It covers subjects like human development, social behaviour and the cognitive process, including knowledge about perceptions.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: A person who is equipped with knowledge of Psychology will likely be able to develop an awareness of himself or herself, as well those around him or her.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Psychology is also very relevant in the current context, not only to counter the manipulation of minds in relation to radicalism, but also for other social ills that arise from the usage of social media.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: We have seen many situations where conflicts arise in social media due to different perspectives and perceptions about current issues and sensitive issues.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Often, it descends into insults, through the use of inappropriate words and phrases.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe that, with a knowledge of Psychology that is obtained in school, this will enable one to have an open mind, because the person understands that it is natural for different perspectives and perceptions to exist, and we should practise mutual respect when encountering such differences.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As the Malay saying goes, "we will have dark hair, but we have different hearts" which, in English, means, "we can agree to disagree".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Aside from imparting religious values and learning psychology, the inculcation of community and national values is also important.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In our country, the inculcation of community and national values is done in schools through the National Education subject.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The racial riots of the past are a grim reminder of what it can be like if there is no mutual trust and understanding among different societal groups.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have developed a Singaporean approach that worked for us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Although it is not perfect, we have enjoyed decades of peace and harmony.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In late 2015, I attended a seminar called "Celebrating Humanity, Faith and Love".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It was organised by Jamiyah Singapore, held in Soka Association in Tampines, and attended by Muslims, Buddhists, Christians, Taoists and Freethinkers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I stood at the rostrum and could not help but marvel at the miracle that we have created.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: A week ago, I attended the 100th Anniversary of the Sheng Hong Temple and it was well-attended by leaders of Singapore's major faiths.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are probably one of the few places in the world where this can happen regularly, celebrated widely, and perhaps even taken for granted at times.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have forged a common space where Singaporeans can practise their faiths freely.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Extremists can then lay claim that multiculturalism just does not work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The chaos and destruction from a successful terrorist attack in Singapore will drive wedges right along our fault lines.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Will we unite and overcome the challenges together as one Singapore, or will we crumble and fall apart?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The ties that we have nurtured during peaceful times can hopefully endure such a test.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Even though we have differences, I believe that what divides us pales in comparison to what unites us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, this is something that we should not take for granted, especially when terrorism is almost at our doorstep.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is imperative that we strengthen our bulwark against these winds of evil.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have certainly made much progress through our many emergency preparedness programmes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This reminds us that we have our work cut out for us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can we further scale our efforts, especially in schools and workplaces?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The social media is an important battleground that must be won.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Social media has a critical role to play in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It can be an agent in uniting or dividing us.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the event of such an incident, these "online first responders" could be the first ones to put out their thoughts and, hence, lead discussions in a productive manner.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If there are groups that try to spread falsehoods or rumours online that can confuse the public in times of chaos, these "first responders" could help Government agencies spread the correct messages to resolve the issue.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I will next touch on fighting hate speech and extremist thinking.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Incidents in other countries have shown a growing trend of extremist thinking.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must not allow our people to be influenced by these unhealthy trends which will create fear and suspicion among different races and religions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must not only counter these perceptions online but also in our private lives daily.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It can be when a family member makes a careless remark to us, or when a friend circulates such messages through WhatsApp or other means of communication.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must stand up to such seemingly innocent but are really soft approaches of spreading division and disunity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have a duty, both moral and national, to not participate in spreading such messages.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While Singapore has laws to curb hate speech, such legislation may not be the only or the best way to deal with such matters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The safety and security that we have enjoyed for many decades are not something that came about by chance, but it is a result of hard work over a long period of time.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government's strong and consistent enforcement of the law, a dedicated and capable Home Team and SAF, and the forward-looking social policies have kept terrorism at bay.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have been fortunate thus far to be spared from terrorist attacks.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The threat is real and we must all play our part in being vigilant in our daily lives.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Since young, through education, every Singaporean has been continuously reminded that the peace and stability that we enjoy should not be taken for granted.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is vital for all of us to look out for security threats and to know how to respond to such threats.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We should acknowledge that terrorism is not far away and it can come to Singapore in both physical and psychological forms.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We should not think of it as "if it happens", that is, if terrorism comes to Singapore, but rather think of it as "when it happens", what do we do?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Are we prepared to confront it or hide behind the veil of fear and trepidation?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Our Singapore workforce constituents comprise a combination of local and migrant workers.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, it is not only important to inculcate the value of multiracialism and multiculturalism among Singaporeans, but also to the migrant workers from various countries.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With such diversity in the workplace, it is pertinent to place emphasis on workplace integration and management of diversity.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There should be platforms for the employees to understand the local culture, and this should be an integral part of the organisation, such as during employee orientation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For example, I would like to quote some positive examples from Khoo Teck Puat Hospital.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As the President of Healthcare Services Employees' Union (HSEU), I have attended as an invited guest to their festive celebrations, such as Chinese New Year, Hari Raya Puasa, Deepavali, to mention a few.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I am so heartened and impressed by the efforts put in by the management of all levels, including doctors, to integrate their staff from various cultural backgrounds.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is strongly supported by the Chief Executive Officer and the Senior Management staff.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The event is designed in a manner that the audience understands the rationale as well as the practices of each culture.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The entire event, including the emcees and performers, are employees of Khoo Teck Puat Hospital.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The organisers, who are employees themselves, take a deep interest in trying to understand the cultural practices and translate them into easily comprehensible acts or performance to the audience, that is, their diverse employees.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, during the period of Ramadan, non-Muslim employees were encouraged to fast for one day so that they can participate in the fasting process with their Muslim colleagues and, at the same time, understand the reasons for doing so.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In this case, it is beyond theory but also in action, showing the unique practices of each culture.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, at this year's Hari Raya Puasa celebration at Khoo Teck Puat Hospital, our hon Parliamentary Secretary, Mr Amrin Amin, was the special guest at the event.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: He can concur that the kind of enthusiasm, high spirit and atmosphere of gotong royong amongst the staff of all races and nationalities dressed up in the traditional Malay outfits were, indeed, highly commendable.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The above example is an illustration of how organisations can weave in the workplace integration efforts as part of their staff inclusiveness in the social setting.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, I personally feel that the organisers need to put in dedicated time to design the programme in a style that the audience can capture the essence of workplace integration and harmony.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As we go through the major economic transformation, it is vital that we focus on both the hardware and the heartware so that our social fabrics at workplaces are strengthened.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Similar to how we treat health and safety as an important value and culture at our workplaces, likewise, workplace integration and harmony must be regarded and treated with equal importance for Singapore's progress, not only in today's global climate, but also for tomorrow.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: While we place great emphasis on workplace integration and inclusion, it is of paramount importance that we always stay guarded against the potential threat that confronts us, be it in the community or at the workplaces, and be better prepared to confront the threat and overcome the fear.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The employees must be trained to be conscious of their surroundings and be better prepared to identify potential dangers, such as strange behaviours of their fellow employees or strangers loitering at the workplace.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There must be an independent channel for staff to raise alert should there be a likelihood of threat, and that companies must be willing and be prepared to deal with such alerts.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Workplaces must continue to maintain harmony, and it is the corporate social responsibility of every employer to do so.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In the event such threats should happen despite much vigilance, companies must have the means to deal with the recovery to attain the normalcy state swiftly.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For this, it is crucial for companies to have professionals who could better address the psychology of employees who are affected.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Incidences at workplaces should not divide a society or stigmatise people based on race, religion or nationality.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to preserve harmony and industrial peace, as societal disruption is a perfect recipe for a country's downfall.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I would urge the Government to encourage and, where required, mandate the following to prepare workplaces better to confront terrorism.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Companies must be well-connected and work with various Government agencies, such as the Singapore Civil Defence Force, Home Team, as well as healthcare institutions at a geographical cluster level.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The availability of professionals, such as psychotherapists, psychologists and professional counsellors, will certainly be of great help in identifying individuals who are much affected, both mentally and behaviourally, so that early intervention will certainly defuse potential explosive threats from taking place.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
