text: It will also prevent such vulnerable individuals from being preyed upon by terrorist cells.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: When incidents happen, the workers have only themselves to help one another until rescue comes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Companies must invest in this effort to train their employees for the possible eventuality.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Companies should also encourage their employees to support blood donation and be prepared to do so when called upon.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The unions in the unionised companies can partner this effort.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The challenge is to sustain the effort and, essentially, to remind ourselves that the threat is constant and psychological preparedness is key.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It has no nationality, race, religion, language nor gender.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But perhaps none has been more potent or devastating than those who have espoused their warped cause, falsely and illegitimately, in the name of religion in recent times.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Terrorism cannot claim to represent any particular religion, it has nothing to do with religion, it is plain and simply born out of warped human fundamentalism.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Islam, like all mainstream religions, is a religion of peace.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, various groups like Al-Qaeda, ISIS, all claim the right to inflict wrongs and inflict it on their Muslim brothers and sisters and establish an Islamic Caliphate, which they promise will be heaven on earth, but it is more like hell.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But from what I have read and learnt from my Muslim friends, Islam does not support terrorism.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Islam calls upon Muslims to submit to the will of God.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, terrorists have misappropriated the words of the Quran for their own agenda.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Their actions are completely at odds with the message contained in the Quran.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fundamentalism, therefore, has no place in our present world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Adherence to a strict, literal interpretation of scripture does more harm than good to mankind.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And just because we can pick and choose and memorise particular verses from the Quran, the Bible, the Torah and any other religious text does not make us religious at all.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Religion, in fact, provides all of us with a pathway to be better human beings.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fundamentalism, on the other hand, leads one towards the corruption of the human soul.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A little knowledge is a dangerous thing, they say.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This terrorist, who was neither religiously inclined nor formally trained, was infused with deviant thoughts and teachings while in the Middle East.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But, if we consider this very carefully, he is but one of the many Muslim, Christian, Jewish, Buddhist or Hindu youths who are now being influenced by deviant teachings widely available on social media and the Dark Web.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is, therefore, incumbent upon all Singaporeans to be on a look-out to report family members, friends and individuals who display signs of having been radicalised in their thoughts and actions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They will be doing not only themselves and our nation a favour but also the affected individuals as well.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Betterment of society is the key word and I am glad that MUIS, in the same sermon on 29 September, preached that Muslims will continue to contribute to the prosperity and development of the community that they are living in.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore is blessed that it has enlightened Muslim leaders who are in sync with the larger good of the community.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Their enlightened and progressive approach to many issues, such as organ donations, the Milk Bank, cord blood donations, only serves to strengthen our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One can only imagine the havoc that can be created by self-serving rouge teachers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The ARS' emphasis on contextualising around a multiracial and multi-religious societal core is also an important development.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I hope that other religious communities in Singapore would also be able to mould their own religious teachings in the same way.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Ultimately, deviant teachings serve two purposes: to turn the follower against the world and the world against the followers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Feeding the cycle of hate and fundamentalism only makes the world a far more restive and tense place, where every action can spark the tinder box of suspicion and violence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But even after more than 50 years of nationhood, this is still fragile.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This calls for all of us to think very hard.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Prime Minister, in his recent Kopi Talk, highlights this concern aptly.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The social cohesion and racial harmony that we are enjoying now are not a given.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It needs nurturing; it needs tender loving care because harmony, Mr Speaker, Sir, is not a luxury for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is an absolute necessity for our very existence as a nation, as a people.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, how do we go about nurturing racial harmony among Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By getting them more involved and interacting with Singaporeans of all races and religions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Schools could take a greater lead in this by encouraging students to interact with students of other races not just on the surface, but more in-depth and an understanding of the cultures and traditions and what motivates them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This really needs to start at a young age.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our leaders have also been emphasising Singapore's potential as a prime target for terrorists.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Minister Shanmugam's recent statement that there is still some way to go for terror preparedness among Singaporeans is also worrying.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The SGSecure movement is already a year old.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Preparation for any eventuality has been a way of life for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of my fellow hon Members have mentioned different aspects of this.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, these five key areas have stood us in good stead over the years but how prepared will we be for the actual event, when it happens?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, we need to focus also a lot on psychological preparedness which needs a lot of work.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We talk about unity in diversity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is these that we must be weary of.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is quite one thing to be proud of what you believe in and quite another to use that pride to deride another's beliefs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For many of us in this Chamber, as members of the majority race, it may seem hard to comprehend.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some people have asked me why I have constantly worn a lapel pin of the Singapore flag.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have done this since I was in university.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I studied in the United Kingdom (UK) and it was in the university overseas that, for the first time, I was not the majority race.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It was also the first time I experienced what it meant to be a minority.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It was not violent, it was not always in your face, but it was always there lurking.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Regardless of my actual surname, to many of the shopkeepers in town, I was a Ching, Chang and Chong and they never did it with any sort of malice, it was always with a smile.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Regardless of my actual nationality, I have been called a communist from the mainland or a boat boy from Saigon.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And regardless of my faith, I was a papist practising popery in the Anglican heartland.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Again, none of this was in your face, but it was always there.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It was always slightly percolating beneath the surface.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I found comfort in the community in church but I did not retreat away.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To be honest, I was angry when I first experienced this, but I was encouraged to do something positive about it.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And so, I ran for the Students Union as the Ethnic Minorities Officer, won the seat and then served on the Chaplaincy reaching out to other minorities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And because of those experiences, I also started wearing the flag as a visible sign to others and also a reminder to myself.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Today, back here, in Singapore, I belong to the majority race.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I still wear the flag as a reminder that there is much work for us to do.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How do our brother and sister Singaporeans from minority races cope because I am sure they faced the same difficulties I did overseas and, perhaps, even to a deeper level because it is not violent, it is not always in your face.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not always apparent but it is there.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have also discovered that the worst that we can do is to retreat into our own false security of our small racial and religious circles.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because it is only when we reach out that we can reach in to strengthen our own identities.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can have pride in who we are, but it is in the sharing and learning of others' cultures and practices that we can fully appreciate our very own.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are buffeted on all sides by deviant thoughts, we are drawn towards the seductive call of separatism, of living apart from others.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But I also see in Singapore a horizon filled with bright lights.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While our very existence as an oasis of harmony is also the reason for us to be targets but it is also our harmony that will bind us closer together should something happen because we are Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As One People United, we can weather any storm.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, Mr Speaker, Sir, I support this Motion wholeheartedly and I pledge to do my own small part so that all of us can stay united against any threat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When we were trying to get out of the colonial mess of divide and rule, using race to split the people in Malaya, our founding patriots in the 1950s pledged on unconditional multiracialism to bring peace and security to our land.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The image of "Merdeka" that is burned into my mind is the image of the four main races linking arms in solidarity and marching forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: More than anyone else, the late S Rajaratnam had been the one who defined our foundational multiracialism in the 1960s.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He saw the four main races of our nation as four independent circles brought together by history, now overlapping in terms of social bonds, cultural practices and political and economic interests, creating a common space in the middle of the overlap that could be called truly and uniquely Singaporean.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The task of our multiracial nation-building was to keep working at enlarging that common space.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the 1980s, because society was becoming very individualistic and uneven competition was leading to some groups being left behind in education and employment, the emphasis shifted to bolstering community bonds and identities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The consciousness and appreciation of our cultural heritage was promoted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Then, in the 2000s, there was another shift.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One speech that I like to quote in my own academic papers is that of Minister of Community Development and Sports Yaacob Ibrahim's speech at the Wee Kim Wee Seminar on cross-cultural understanding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In that speech, he mapped out what he saw as the third phase of the evolution of our multiracialism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Multiculturalism is also about us Singaporeans adopting and modifying cultural values and practices from one another so that we become more like one another and yet, still diverse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He said, "When a Malay colleague of mine invited me to his home to have a steamboat dinner, my understanding of what it means to be Malay in Singapore had to be updated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When I visit Komala Vilas with my family and tuck into the vegetarian food, the crowd there is truly varied and Singaporean." This 2003 speech on multiculturalism is important, given the historical context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It came in the wake of the 9/11 attacks in New York and the arrest of the JI members in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Multiculturalism signalled to Singaporeans and the world we would not adopt reactionary approaches that could lead to backlash, we would not stigmatise any particular community and turn neighbours on neighbours with suspicion and phobia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, we would fortify our multiracialism foundations to promote inclusivity, harmony and cross-cultural dialogue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The situation is not too different today, except that terror is now cellular and social mediatised, harder to detect and more unpredictable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is tempting to turn the institutions and social capital Singaporeans have built up into security instruments to counter terrorism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I would like to sound a warning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Multiracialism gives us the firm ground for us to stand and fight extremist threats to our nation; we do not tear up our ground to use as stones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will heighten racial thinking and we will risk unintended consequences.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A weaponised multiracialism will not only hold back progress to our post-racial aspiration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It can also turn xenophobic and be used against the many migrant communities and cultures that have come to our shores.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A weaponised multiracialism can cause race consciousness to feed on itself, leading people to judge one another on the basis of race, making us ask one another and ourselves: what makes a Chinese-Singaporean Chinese, whether a Malay-Singaporean is Malay enough, when an Indian-Singaporean is acceptable as family and leader?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, we need to strengthen our foundation and invest in multiracialism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is much to learn from the past, even as we celebrate the present and prepare for the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Returning to the 2003 speech by Minister Yaacob, we should start to think about the next phase of evolution of our multiracialism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to build on the inclusive multiculturalism that was adopted in the 2000s to deepen it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As Minister Yaacob said in 2003, the evolution did not happen by design but by choice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have to be careful not to over-engineer the evolution, or we cause multiracialism to become irrelevant or, worse, cause people to lose faith in multiracialism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have to look at the choices we have now on the ground.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, what choices do we have on the ground?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What choices are being made by our grassroots multiracial institutions on the ground?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are three examples I would like to highlight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The name "self-help group centre" is actually an oxymoron.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The centre will become a mutual support centre, where Singaporeans of different races seek to help one another to overcome their difficulties in life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is no longer communal self-help as we know it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The self-help groups are fast becoming mutual help groups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This captures the movement on the ground, the choices that Singaporeans, originally caught up in their orientation towards their own community, are making.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans are choosing to forge trans-racial ties, that is, creating social bonds that transcend racial identities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And Singaporeans are choosing to engage in intercultural exchange and, that is, doing cultural practices across ethnic lines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The setting up of multicultural help centres in all Community Hubs would be more beneficial to the Singaporeans needing help than to rent out public grassroots spaces to private tuition centres.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our proposal also goes further to call for the IRCCs to be enhanced to operate as programme providers at the multicultural help centres.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We also proposed a coordinating secretariat be set up within the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) to help oversee the work of the centres.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This coordinating secretariat could transform Community Development Councils (CDCs) into regional offices for multicultural programme resources and services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would greatly extend the impact and reach of the inclusive and collaborative multiculturalism being pioneered by the self-help groups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of the problems that groups promoting collaborative multiculturalism face is the lack of knowledge of innovative methodologies for cross-cultural exchanges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another problem is the lack of knowledge of content materials, such as best practices and case studies of successful cross-cultural collaborations to solve community problems, that could be used for the workshops and enrichment programmes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Cultural studies is an important field of study that would increase the capacity of the self-help groups to collaborate with one another, but cultural studies is still an underdeveloped academic field in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One of the reasons for the success of multiculturalism in diverse, migrant societies is the emphasis on multicultural practices and pedagogy in schools.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Teachers are the frontline officers in this effort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They could inspire students to multicultural values or cause cynicism reinforcing racial thinking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: National education programmes can only do so much with its content-rich approach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Teachers are the real-life role models for students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Teachers should receive special training in multicultural pedagogy so that they can better engage students from different backgrounds and bring together them for effective cross-cultural interactions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Schools can also work closely with self-help groups in their multicultural help centres, so that multicultural practices would not be limited to performances and food but involve real-time collaboration to tackle real-life issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have built up important institutions and a rich cache of social capital since.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, as we confront extremism, as we always have, I hope the Government will resist the temptation to weaponise multiracialism as instruments to counter terror.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Multiracialism is only effective for countering extremism when it is not treated as a measure and means to counter extremism, but respected as an end in itself, the good that defines the essence of who we are as Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to look to the ground to see the features of the next phase of evolution of our multiracialism.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Deepen the trans-racial collaboration and intercultural interactions, and we would be one step closer to our post-racial aspirations.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Extremism in the name of religion and race has brought fear and death in its wake.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But just as dangerous are exclusivist beliefs and segregationist practices that result in communities not only staying apart from one another but making no effort to understand one another.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: These are societies in which the views of one community about the other are informed only by stereotype or prejudice.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: On the surface, all may appear calm and peaceful, sometimes for years.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But when groups segregate themselves from others, social harmony is easily lost and hard to recover.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: So, when a crisis hits, when a terrorist attacks, or when times are tough, such societies can fall apart.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The extremism of ISIS has also spawned another monster, that of Islamophobia, in the West.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Far-right groups in the West are gaining political ground by openly campaigning against Muslims.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: All of us, regardless of race or religion, must squarely face and defeat this trifecta of disunity and not let it take root in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: As a country founded on multiracialism where all races live together in mutual respect and equality, this is a threat to our very existence as a nation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: As a minority in a plural society, our Malay/Muslim community and its leaders are acutely aware of the challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Racial riots defined the fears of our founding generation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Our community's Pioneers saw clearly the importance of a united and strong society, where all communities are well-integrated.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Earlier this year, during my annual Hari Raya function with community leaders, I emphasised how the Malay/Muslim community has faced evolving challenges with resolve.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In the aftermath of 9/11 and the uncovering of the plot of JI members planning terror attacks in the region and at home, there was intense scrutiny of the community.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Yet, the community and our religious leaders rallied together to tackle this threat, along with the rest of Singapore society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Over the past decade, our community has enhanced the capabilities of our religious teachers, or asatizahs, strengthened the curriculum of our madrasahs and revamped the delivery of part-time religious education to meet the needs of the community.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We have the RRG, initiated and led by senior asatizahs who volunteered themselves as counsellors to help rehabilitate and reintegrate radicalised individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We launched the Harmony Centre@An-Nahdhah mosque in Bishan and supported inter-faith dialogues.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: To live out the ideals of Islam as a religion of peace, we created the Rahmatan Lil Alamin Foundation, or Blessings to All Foundation, to aid universal humanitarian causes to bring aid to Muslims and non-Muslims alike.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The emergence of ISIS-inspired ideologues and extremists and their methods of operation have magnified the challenge ahead of us.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Their sophisticated use of the Internet, coinciding with the ubiquity of Internet access, influence and corrupt the impressionable and gullible.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Similarly, such contents help plant the seeds of doubt and fear in non-Muslims.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The security agencies have put in tremendous efforts to safeguard our country against terrorism.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: They have stepped up vigilance and, in recent months, have issued detention orders to radicalised individuals who planned to travel to Syria to fight for ISIS.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But beyond law and enforcement, ultimately, it is a battle for the hearts and minds of all Singaporeans, whether Muslim or non-Muslim.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The Malay/Muslim community, on our part, has stepped up efforts to address this triple threat to our social cohesion and national security.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Allow me, Sir, to highlight the key thrusts of the community efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: One major thrust of our community efforts is to develop a corps of religious leaders and teachers who provide the community with sound guidance and who can counter dangerous ideologies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Our asatizahs can act as a bulwark against extremist and segregationist ideologies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: They play a key role in guiding our local Muslims in practising their faith in accordance with the context of a multiracial and multi-religious Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Central to the ARS status is the need for all asatizahs to abide by a Code of Ethics, which includes not denigrating any racial or religious group.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Anyone who crosses the line will be dealt with decisively.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: One example is Rasul bin Dahri, a Singaporean preacher who is not ARS-recognised but published books on Islamic doctrine.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: This action, Sir, shows that we have zero tolerance for individuals and publications that promote ill-will among different groups.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: MUIS encourages these asatizahs to continuously upgrade themselves, under the Continuous Professional Education (CPE), and organises various training platforms, including modules on "moderation in religion", counselling workshops on developing engaged families and learning journeys to the RRG.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Many of our asatizahs receive their training in renowned overseas Islamic universities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: With this, our community will be able to train a new generation of asatizahs here.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: At the same time, MUIS will strive to learn and adapt best practices from the best Islamic universities in the world to our local context.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: To do so, we need to tailor programmes that cater to the different segments of the community.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The aLIVE programme, an acronym for "Living Islamic Values Everyday", is an age-appropriate and interactive class for children aged nine to 16.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: For the working adults, MUIS has designed ADIL, or Adult Islamic Learning, which includes modules about the universal Islamic values and ethics, such as mutual respect between among communities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: To address the serious concern of online radicalisation, MUIS has started parenting seminars to advise parents on issues, such as authenticating online Islamic content and dealing with digital addiction among children and youths.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Earlier on, Sir, I touched on the establishment of RRG in 2003 to rehabilitate radicalised individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: RRG has, over the years, expanded its role in building social resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: RRG has organised briefings, forums and dialogues to educate both Muslims and non-Muslims about key Islamic concepts that have been perverted by terrorists and extremist groups.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: RRG has also published content online to explain and debunk the fallacies of ISIS ideologies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It also offers over-the-phone counselling through its RRG helpline.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: RRG also launched a Resource and Counselling Centre at Khadijah Mosque in Geylang to provide training and resources to RRG counsellors, asatizahs and members of the public who are interested to do research on extremism.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: RRG has hosted over 1,500 visitors, ranging from foreign delegates to students and community groups.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The recent arrests of radicalised Singaporeans have highlighted how family and friends could see how a loved one was becoming radicalised, but not refer these individuals for help.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We have a number of our asatizahs who have a strong online presence and have youth-centric programmes that appeal to the young.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We want to work with them so that they can serve as the "first line of response" to guide these youths seeking answers and address incipient leanings towards problematic ideologies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The more serious cases will be referred to RRG for rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: As for the general public, from time to time, MUIS prepares Friday sermons, as Mr Alex Yam has noted, specifically to educate the community on the threats of ISIS and radical ideologies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Topics include dispelling the notion of the call for armed jihad, condemning ISIS and how it is undermining Islam, and emphasising moderation in Islam.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: MUIS also works with RRG in conducting pre-sermon talks covering themes, such as cyber wellness, building resilience against extremist and exclusivist ideologies, and the importance of looking out to save friends or family who may be falling under the influence of radical ideology.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It has been a difficult and challenging journey for my community.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Tharman recently said at the NTU Majulah Lecture, "growing up as a minority is different from growing up as a majority…never pretend that it's the same".

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Sometimes, the majority does not know what it feels to be a minority community.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: And for the Malay/Muslim community, this sense of being misunderstood is deeply felt, having been in the spotlight for quite some time.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It is not a pleasant experience when your religion and your religious orientation are under constant scrutiny.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: When other faith communities stepped forward to lend support to our struggle, it gave us comfort that we are not in this alone.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: So, while Muslims have come under scrutiny in recent times, Singaporeans recognised that it is not only our community's battle, it is everyone's battle.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: So, I was glad, like Mr Pritam Singh, when our Singaporean Buddhist brothers recently stepped forward to lend support to Singaporean Muslims who felt a sense of anguish for the situation in Rakhine state in Myanmar.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: They did so, despite sharing a common faith with the majority in Myanmar.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Each and every one of us is a part of Singapore, and we are interconnected in many different ways, linked through history, living side by side in our neighbourhoods, schools, workplaces, recreational activities and, sometimes, through marriage.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: These connections are the social glue that binds us together as a nation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We all sing the same national anthem and hold our right fist to our hearts when reciting the pledge.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: These, and many other experiences of being a Singaporean, must mean something to every one of us, especially when the going gets tough for a member of the Singaporean family.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We must all work together to ensure that we preserve a cohesive Singapore society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We can defeat extremism, exclusivism and Islamophobia and other threats only if we feel for one another and do whatever we can to tackle these challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We require a Team Singapore approach that must become our way of life.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We must build friendships and strong bonds among different communities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: With solid foundations of mutual understanding and respect, different communities will stand by and help one another.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Through the good work of our community organisations, the grassroots and the IRCCs in every constituency, religious and community leaders regularly come together to network and collaborate on projects that help members of different communities work together for common causes.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Nevertheless, we need more individuals to step forward in and outside of social media to reach out to as many as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We need netizens to speak up with moral clarity against injustice and stereotypes, and those who promote hatred and intolerance.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Earlier this year, I met Noor Mastura, co-founder of Interfaith Youth Circle, who organises inter-religious dialogues and engagements in safe spaces to better understand one another's religions and traditions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Last year, I met Muzakkir Samat, who co-edited a book "From Walden to Woodlands", an interfaith anthology of poetry about nature in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: I understand that the Nanyang Confucian Association in Singapore has organised three Chinese-language forums on "Confucianism and Islam" earlier this year and in June last year to raise the level of understanding of Islam in the Chinese community.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The Singapore Buddhist Lodge donates rice to mosques annually before Ramadan to be cooked for the breaking of fast and distributed to needy families.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We need more to step up and reach out across the boundaries of race and religion.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The Government can and must deter wrongdoing with laws, and we can support with resources and advice, but we need good people, like Noor Mastura and Muzakkir Samat, to come forward to take action and build bridges across communities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We need Singaporeans to make racial and religious harmony happen in the everyday, through the friendships that are forged in school, in the workplaces and at play, and the deeper understanding that can happen when we try to discover and appreciate a little more about beliefs and customs different from our own.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It is through the sum of all these efforts that we can become a stronger, more resilient and more harmonious society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: (In Malay):    Mr Speaker, the global community is currently struggling with extremism that threatens our harmony and social cohesion.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: At the same time, we face certain groups which adopt exclusivist practices and isolate themselves, to the point that when a crisis occurs, it will result in divisions within society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We, in Singapore, are not immune to such threats.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: As a small country that is multi-religious and multiracial in nature, we have no choice other than to strengthen our country's resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: As a minority in Singapore's plural society, the Malay/Muslim community and its leaders have always steadfastly upheld the principle of solidarity where all communities integrate well.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The dark chapter in our history, when racial riots took place prior to Singapore's Independence, was a lesson for our Pioneer leaders.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Although security agencies have enhanced enforcement measures, this is not enough.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Every Singaporean, whether Muslim or non-Muslim, has a role to ensure that terrorist ideologies do not spread here.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Over the past few years, the Malay/Muslim community has enhanced efforts to contribute towards Singapore's resilience, especially in two areas of strengthening religious leadership and forging a more comprehensive community engagement.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In the effort to strengthen religious leadership, it is important that our religious teachers are empowered to guide the community in practising religious teachings that are appropriate to our context of multiracial and multi-religious life in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In addition, we are also increasing efforts to enhance community engagement through programmes that are appropriate for all ages.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In fact, other organisations also play a role to counter terrorism.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: For instance, RRG has done a lot to engage Muslims and non-Muslims through community programmes as well as by providing information online.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: This effort must continue in order to further strengthen understanding and mutual respect among all races and appreciate our differences.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The biggest victory is when we stay united in the face of any challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Only by doing so can we progress towards a stronger, more resilient and more harmonious society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, we should take heart in what we have achieved so far.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: If we stand together as one, we will keep Singapore, our home, safe and secure for all of us and for the generations to come.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: So, let us continue helping one another, reaching out to one another, and be a blessing to everyone around us.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.35 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.15 pm until 4.35 pm.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: (In Mandarin):   I would like to thank Mr de Souza for this Motion to call for Singaporeans to stay firm and fight the threat of terrorism together.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, terror attacks in other countries have become unpredictable, like the many lone-wolf attacks that had happened in Europe and the US.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We know it is impossible to have 100% security assurance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is equally important is the preparedness at the people's level.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should be prepared at the psychological level and build resilience and mutual trust among different races.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to focus on how to cope with the "Day after" effect and recover quickly and resume our normal life as fast as possible.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For the past 50 years, we have been fortunate in that we have not experienced any serious racial or religious conflicts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is due to the continuous efforts of the Government as well as people of the various races.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Most Singaporeans recognise the importance of living in harmony and social stability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, they respect and tolerate one another, mind the sensitivity of different races and respect the differences.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we also know that Singapore's social harmony and resilience have not really been tested by a major incident.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have also introduced the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act to strengthen the legal framework to ensure social harmony.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We put in place EIP for HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In order to have enough representation of minority groups in Parliament, we have implemented the Group Representation Constituency (GRC) system.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have self-help groups for different ethnic groups to create a caring and harmonious multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of course, we can further strengthen our legislation and policies, such as focusing on solving upstream problems.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we also know that it is not enough to rely on policies and laws alone to build strong and long-lasting trust and a harmonious relationship.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to further strengthen the relationship among different races by working harder in the communities, schools and workplaces to build mutual trust and confidence.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Fortunately, our Pioneers had the firm belief that a multiracial Singapore must be built upon strong social harmony.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By setting up the People's Association (PA), we have created grassroots organisations which can bring together residents and promote a harmonious relationship among people of different backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The purpose of grassroots organisations is to build more common spaces in the community, facilitating residents of different races to have more opportunities to interact and build rapport.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Promoting integration and harmony does not mean that we will neglect our own cultural heritage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We will continue to promote the culture of different races and this will help different races to appreciate and understand one another's culture.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Seeking consensus while allowing differences is a sustainable way to bring different races together and make our multicultural society attractive.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Based on this, we can deepen our interactions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During the engagement and the interaction process among different races, we can adopt light-hearted ways that are close to people's daily life to build rapport and trust.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In recent years, I noticed that while we have a stronger awareness of tolerance and the need to respect one another's differences and sensitivities, we have become more reluctant to discuss issues concerning race and religion at the personal level.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, many people do not know how to talk about these issues with friends or neighbours.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are worried that if they say something inappropriately, they may offend friends of a different race or religion.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If this situation continues, or people only say politically correct things, not only will it not help build the trust, but hinder the efforts to build a long-lasting bond.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A strong, long-lasting bond is, in fact, the key to whether a society can withstand a major incident.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should create more opportunities and an environment whereby Singaporeans can have sincere and candid discussions concerning race and religion without much inhibition.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Grassroots and other community organisations have provided a very good platform.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should make good use of these platforms and expand the scope of interaction, plan engaging and interesting dialogues to deepen understandings amongst us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am pleased to see that Singapore has enlightened and well-respected religious and community leaders.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They continuously contribute to the country and our unity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is more, they all know the importance of the overall interest of the country and speak out when necessary.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They also condemn terrorism without hesitation to protect our harmony.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although what they say may be criticised or even attacked by their own community, they do not shirk.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This has demonstrated our community and religious leaders' courage and faith.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Just now, I listened to Dr Yaacob's speech.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I can imagine the stress and challenges faced by our Muslim community leaders.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Parliament, we often see Mr Masagos and Dr Yaacob speaking up on sensitive policies that could affect the Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Their stance is firm and they have never shirked.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Building a harmonious society is an endless journey.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should see this as something that can enrich our lives, broaden our views, and a unique Singapore way of life.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The key is to promote unity in a natural and sustainable way and not to see it as a burden.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, I would like to congratulate the hon Member for Holland-Bukit Timah Mr Christopher de Souza for introducing this Motion to this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I fully agree with the points that he made in his speech and I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The specific focus in my speech is on two overlapping areas identified in the Motion: preventing the spread of radicalised teaching that promotes exclusivity and violent extremism; and investing in multiracialism to inoculate ourselves against the ills of extremism and terrorism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One preliminary point which I want to discuss first though is: what exactly is meant by "multiracialism" as a policy?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The common refrain is that we forge a common life whilst we preserve our own separate heritage and identity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Does that mean that we are required to put Singapore ahead of our own individual backgrounds and heritage?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It may be useful to refer to the objectives of our founding fathers who embarked on this journey of multiracialism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I heard my learned friend, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh's worry about weaponising multiracialism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand his concerns but I would not be too worried because, really, the reference to multiracialism as a social weapon is a call to arms on the part of the people to put in their energies to invest in multiracialism as a policy that will bring peace to our country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also wish to highlight an excerpt of Mr George Yeo's speech at the inauguration of the Association of Muslim Professionals in 1991.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said as follows: "We use the term 'multiracialism' so often that we sometimes forget what it means.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It does not mean that in becoming Singaporean, we deny our heritage…That is not acceptable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Part of the essence of being Singaporean is the right to retain our separate ethnic character.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But that right carries a corresponding duty to accept that others of other races also have the same rights." This is not a theoretical musing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A good understanding of the underpinnings of multiracialism policy will help us formulate the responses we need to make as a society to issues pertaining to extremism and terrorism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will now proceed to deal with some of these issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the topic of preventing radicalisation through radicalised teachings and other modes, means or methods, it may be useful to take a step back and understand what are the contributing factors that promote radicalisation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One, socio-economic factors − not being able to improve economically and being trapped in the poverty cycle.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Two, power of radical ideology expoused by charismatic idealogues focusing on exploiting unhappiness amongst a group of people, often leveraging on social media, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Three, presence of oppressed communities in the world, especially along racial and religious lines.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Members who spoke before me also highlighted this point.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Over the years, we have seen that RRG has even upped the scale of resources.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They have set up the Resource and Counselling Centre and a hotline and mobile app to allow better access to the religious teachers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They have also embarked on reaching out to young people through the Internet.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that the RRG teachers and academics are mostly Malay and English-speaking.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the book, Majulah, 50 years of Malay/Muslim Community in Singapore edited by Mr Zainul Abidin Rasheed and Mr Norsharil Saat, there was an interview published of Habib Hassan, the Imam of Baalwie Mosque and an esteemed member of IRO.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have the pleasure of knowing him personally.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said that there is a need to reject teachings that seek to divide Muslims and Muslims, and Muslims and non-Muslims.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In particular, he highlighted there should be no problems in wishing Hindus "Happy Deepavali" and Christians "Merry Christmas".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He also saw a need to evolve a Singaporean model of religious teachings which excludes Middle Eastern culture and politics.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am sure Members of this House will also applaud the concrete steps that have been taken within the Malay/Muslim community to prevent radicalisation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need, however, to recognise that members of other races have a responsibility, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My learned friend, Dr Intan Azura, also spoke about this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I start with the definition of "multiracialism" as a concept in Singapore, because while we have a right to identify ourselves, based on our ethnic background, we also have a duty to recognise and strengthen the bonds and preservation of a common space with members of other races.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: People are not born terrorists; they undergo a process of radicalisation and buying into violent extremist ideology.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is where members of other races and religions have a common duty to reach out to all people of all races, actively promote inclusivity and a sense of common destiny.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As Mr Christopher de Souza said, we live and die here.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have a duty to respect, understand and accept and have a keen interest in one another's culture as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This would be a more holistic response to the trend of radicalisation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All racial and religious communities have a responsibility in preventing radicalisation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now move on to my second area: promoting multiracialism as an instrument against terrorism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On this point, it is noteworthy that across the world, there is a trend of voting towards the Far Right.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While people in Singapore got startled by this, actually, this was predicted in a Pew Research survey published last year in the UK Daily Express on 12 July 2016.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It was entitled "EU nations rejecting multiculturalism − the ISIS effect".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And this caused the rise of the right-wing parties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have had similar trends in other countries, such as in the UK and US.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is exactly what ISIS wants: divide multiracial communities, sow discord and hatred amongst these communities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For that reason alone, it is not difficult to understand why Singapore is a target.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore faces the same danger of populism, majoritarianism, intolerance and racial chauvinism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the 1960s, communal extremism was commonplace in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: President Yusof Ishak referred to them in the same speech I drew this House's attention to earlier.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He pointed out that within 10 weeks of Independence, the communalists were advocating a change in the status of Chinese language because of the large Chinese majority in Singapore, even though Chinese was already one of the four official languages.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not realistic to assume that communal extremism will not rear its head again in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The danger of Islamphobia, in particular, is real.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to ensure politics of responsibility within Singapore when it comes to multiracialism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, across this House, multiracialism is accepted as a pillar of our society and I am heartened by my hon friend Mr Pritam Singh's support of this Motion on behalf of the Workers' Party.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even in relation to the debates on the Elected Presidency issue, both sides of the House acknowledged the wisdom of having Presidents from different races, from time to time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, the bilingual education policy, the four official languages with Malay as the National Language and English as the working language, and the GRC concept, which I say, has the laudable effect of also promoting the emergence and acceptance of multiracial political parties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, there is no guarantee that what is happening in Germany, the UK, US and elsewhere may not happen here.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is the duty of all responsible Singapore political parties to embed in their deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) to resist the temptation to dabble in populist politics, to disavow racial and religious politics, take responsibility when it comes to issues that may potentially give rise to racial and religious tensions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The People's Action Party has made its stance very clear in this regard.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It does not take the current harmonious situation for granted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It always strives to work to strengthen harmony among the races.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And the recent amendments to the Constitution providing for the reserved election for the Elected President is one good example, even though it may be made possibly with a loss of goodwill for the short term.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is also good to ensure that legislative responses to extremism and terrorism are settled now before any serious act of terrorism occurs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have a sound framework of law to deal with major terrorist incidents today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The other area is to deal with obligations to report against a person who is suspected to be a terrorist.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This exposes the society to a danger of what exactly the terrorists want us to be.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He provided me with an analogy which I want to share in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said that Singapore is like a multiracial house built on a foundation of CMIO "bricks".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would say it is CMIEO "bricks", that is, Chinese, Malays, Indians, Eurasians and Others.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result, we have a Singapore that is peaceful, strong and successful.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is this foundation of CMIEO "bricks" that we will have to depend on to weather the effects of extremism and terrorism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We also depend on our uniformed services − the SAF, the Home Team − who are ever ready to protect our countrymen any time any day.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For that, our nation owes them a huge debt.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How will it affect Singapore, the idea of our nation?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Peering at the future from today, we cannot see clearly because the future is always moving, always buffeted by the choices that we make today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I still remember clearly: Block 74, Commonwealth Drive, even though we later moved to a flat in Telok Blangah.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I still remember a few things incredibly clearly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The kids who lived on that corridor − and in those days there were lots of children around − would play on that corridor together.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We would run into one another's flats and spend time there playing and then coming out and running into someone else's flat.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One neighbour, who happened to be Chinese, was good at cutting hair.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: She would cut people's hair for a small fee, but, for us, she would cut our hair for free, the neighbours who lived on the corridor.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I still remember going to her house to cut my hair.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have such a clear memory of this because once there was an Ultra-man television (TV) show playing on the TV while she was doing that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Another memory was that all the children running around downstairs playing with lanterns in our pyjamas during the Mid-Autumn Festival.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Back then, children wore pyjamas and did not shy away from wearing them outside the house.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also remember enjoying lots of good Malay food during Hari Raya.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do children still play in the common corridors these days and mix among different races?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They play football with our neighbour's son and sometimes they play on their scooters.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But, in truth, not as much as I did back in the 1970s.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As I grew up in Singapore, my experience was not much different from other Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I was very fortunate to rarely experience anything like a sense that I was excluded.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I know that not everyone maybe as fortunate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the workplace over the decades, there were times when race issues emerged.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Multiracialism is part of the Singapore pledge which we take as schoolchildren, to be united regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is one of the most important parts of the pledge.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I feel this because when I talk to residents on house visits and outreach, when I look at postings on the Internet, many, many people use the language of the pledge many, many times − that particular bit of language − to express that urge, that aspiration to go beyond race.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At one market outreach last week a resident recited these words several times, emotionally, his voice rising each time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can we set race, religion, culture aside completely?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no complete race blindness, just as there is no complete equality of opportunity for all citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not in Singapore and not in any country.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And there will always be − always − a minority of people for whom attachment to their own identity crosses that line into a close-minded mistrust of others.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But do the majority aspire towards a Singapore, regardless of race?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we must entertain the possibility that it may not be a resounding yes tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the question is how can we nurture, cherish, grow, entrench our multiracial society?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our schools, workplaces, army camps, playgrounds are the crucibles and also the testing grounds of race relations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Multiracialism in the common corridors is just as important as multiracialism in the corridors of power.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The topsoil of multiracialism in Singapore has many colours.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our shared food culture and love of one another's ethnic foods, and this is very important in Singapore's context.
