speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our coffee shops and hawker centres are where all these things come into play.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The bedrock underneath that topsoil is beliefs and attitudes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our willingness to see one another as equal human beings deserving of the same respect we seek for ourselves, our willingness to give and take, to negotiate differences and not to escalate and amplify every single thing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans ask if this structure is as strong today as it was when I played in the common corridor in the 1970s.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But rather than dwell on that subject, I want to focus on the future tense.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have today talked about aspects of policy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In concluding my speech, I would like to talk about some principles that I feel we should hold onto tightly when we formulate, debate, review, replace, evolve policies, projects and initiatives towards multiracialism.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Not that symbols are not important, but I would like to humbly and respectfully offer the opinion that real, everyday issues that affect the day-to-day lives of Singaporeans are more important.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, in school and at work, we do not all start running the race from the same starting line.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And the labour market is not 100% free of prejudice of any kind.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is as it always has been, in Singapore and in every country.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But what we do about that is our choice.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What we do to level up, correct for the inequities of birth and, in so doing, harness all the talent we have.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those are deliberate choices we make as a society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What is at stake is victory or defeat against divisions of class and race, which intersect in complex ways.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us focus on fighting the real battles which are more important than the cosmetic ones.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not want to be complacent about race relations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But implying at every turn that there is a deep, seething primordial tribalism waiting to break out at any time goes too far.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such speech can legitimise the thoughts of the minority who are inclined towards bigotry, a minority that exists − let us recall − in every society and among all races. "See, how I feel is the natural state of human beings," they may say.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And then the minority may influence the majority, one day replacing it.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In speaking of the dangers of getting race relations wrong, let us not go too far and fall into the trap of legitimising and empowering that which we fear.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thirdly, yes, we should not permit − we should never permit − irresponsible racist speech and acts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Civilisation depends on the existence of some boundaries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I want to be absolutely clear about that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we should never draw these boundaries so tightly that responsible discussion of race issues cannot take place in any public platform.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If that happens, people will be cut off from information.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They will not be able to form an educated opinion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will make them more, not less, vulnerable to ignorant and divisive views available on the Internet or in the coffee shops or elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But if we go too far in this, we compromise other values in our pledge.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are a people regardless of race, language and religion to build a democratic society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Whatever we do in the multiracialism arena should always make things better, not make things worse.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our cures must never be worse than the disease.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we must do the right work, do it well and do it as one people.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The day may come when we are all tested.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if that day comes, I am confident that that test will call forth the strength and unity of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That strength, that steel that was forged in our hawker centres, our schools, our army camps, our workplace pantries, our void decks and yes, our common corridors − that steel will prove stronger than any attacker.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We will defend our democratic society regardless of race language and religion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And we will give the gift of multiracialism to future generations of Singaporeans yet unborn.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because we do agree that the threat of terrorism is a very real one and that our defences have to go beyond prevention and rescue.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Not just the day when the attack happens.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We also have to strengthen our social fabric for afterwards.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And that is why I am glad to hear there are lots of agreement that we need to deepen and strengthen our multiracialism in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some see it as a socio-weapon, a steel that helps us stand against those who would divide us.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some see it as defence against globalised forces that would corrupt and poison our society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I see it, first and foremost, as a strength and aspiration.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Love that Singaporeans share for the dream of a multiracial society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A dream that was audacious 50 years ago in the early days of Singapore's existence.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A dream that in many countries seems further and further away.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: A dream that recognises that we are all not perfect, we are all imperfect but that we still believe that we can grow closer to a more perfect union of our people.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is also the love that a child feels for their friends and playmates of different races, religions and cultures.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Children meeting in the void decks of our HDB estates, playing, dancing, learning together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Seeing diversity as something interesting and fulfilling to learn from, without seeing it as a difference.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is also the love that neighbours feel for one another, when they grow closer over the years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That sense of friendship, wanting to grow the shared common space.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is a sense of trust and closeness.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: During my walkabouts in Clementi, I met Mdm Esah, one of our Clementi makciks.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She had a young toddler with her, a young Chinese boy, one year old.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Puan Esah shared that she was helping babysit her neighbour's child during the day because the parents were busy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I was deeply moved by this story, because it is a message of trust and harmony where neighbours of different races trust one another with their children.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is a message that this is your life and mine.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I trust you with my flesh and blood.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But this closeness and friendship and trust, they do not happen spontaneously.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because we know that, in other countries which have taken a free market, laissez-faire, hands-off approach to racial harmony, the outcomes have been very, very unhappy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We saw that in the banlieues in France.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We saw that in Ferguson, Charlottesville, in the US.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because the reality around the world is that, even when the finish line is the same, some have had to walk further and longer just to get to the start.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: By then, my children will be all grown up.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am sure they will have kids of their own by then − my grandchildren.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And I hope that by then, we would have elected a minority candidate as President in an open election.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is something that I am glad that the preceding speaker, Mr Leon Perera, agrees with.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is something I have also been writing about in the TODAY newspaper since 2013, something I raised in my maiden speech last year and in the Budget Debate this year.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have to look at urban design and shared common spaces.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For instance, in some of the newer HDB developments, there are fewer shared spaces for activities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Big sky gardens, but not quite the same.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because when the void deck gets smaller, it can become devoid of interaction.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Seniors passing by, rather than chatting, spending time together in that shared space.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, I call upon the Government to study whether our newer estates will continue to have enough shared common spaces for unstructured, informal interaction.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These design choices can be revenue-neutral, but it makes the difference between a place of transit and a place of friendship and fellowship.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But multiracialism cannot be up to the Government alone.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We should encourage our children to learn about the cultures of other races.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Not because of National Education, not because of an examinable subject, but because it is interesting and part of growing up in multiracial Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can also all learn a little bit of the mother tongues of different communities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In Clementi − and I would say that our Clementi residents are very, very special and exceptional − many of our uncles and aunties know a little bit of Malay.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have met pakciks and makciks who speak a little bit of Hokkien.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have even met a Chinese resident in Clementi who can converse in fluent Tamil.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: All this helps people feel closer and grow closer together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It matters because our lived experience shapes our racial harmony.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It protects against wrong impressions that could arise from social media.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It also ensures a single incident, if it occurs, will not colour someone's perception of other communities for life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, our Malay community and MUIS have resolutely declared openly that Singapore's Muslims are against extremism.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As the saying goes, "a close neighbour is better than a distant relative".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In our HDB estates, neighbours are from different races, religions and background.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Since Independence, we have been living together harmoniously and peacefully for decades, and racial harmony is cherished and recognised by everybody.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: However, this kind of harmony does not come naturally, nor by chance.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If we look back in history and look at the other countries' experience in recent years, we can see that racial conflicts and confrontations are happening again and again.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our national pledge reflects our people's aspirations for and emphasis on racial harmony.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must take concrete actions to fulfil our pledge.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Otherwise, even if we recite it a thousand times, it will be nothing but empty talk.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is something that we should be proud of, cherish and defend.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the past few decades, many economists have realised that a total free market or laissez-faire approach is not necessarily a good thing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the social market, there is also the risk of market failure.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If the younger generations are deprived of the opportunities to know friends from other races, the consequences can be serious.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If our kids can only get to know the other races through the media, particularly, social media, then their understanding of the other races will be very shallow.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Then, how are we going to foster meaningful relationships and build true racial harmony in Singapore?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Maintaining racial harmony is the responsibility of the whole Government, and it is also the responsibility of every citizen and every family.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Although it is said that we must have a nation before we can have a home, we can also build our nation at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We should try our best to create opportunities for our children to make friends with children from other races, whether it is through extra-curricular activities or participation in activities in the HDB estates or community centres.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We should endeavour to create opportunities for children to learn and play together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We can also promote racial harmony through languages.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The mother tongue enables the younger generation to understand their own community's culture, history, tradition and customs.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Likewise, if we learn the languages of the other races, we will be able to understand one another better and our friendship will be deepened.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The racial harmony that Singapore enjoys can be said to be our national treasure.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Let us continue to put in a concerted effort to strengthen racial harmony and fight extremism.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, in July, the Clementi Community Centre (CC) organised a Hari Raya dinner.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We had many friends from different races who came.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We ate a lot, and we chatted a lot.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In June, Clementi CC held a ceremony for new citizens.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We had a demonstration on how to weave ketupats.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The new citizens learned about Singapore's multiracial society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Through activities like these, that is, activities with friends from different races, by learning other cultures and other languages, we can strengthen our racial harmony.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, our multiracialism is the foundation of our past and present.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is what will keep Singapore together the day after an attack happens.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is what will keep Singapore a beacon to the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must strengthen it for today, for our children and their children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He expressed his concerns and asked why Muslims are not doing anything about it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At that juncture, I could not help but feel defensive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I explained to my non-Muslim friend that the terrorists are extremists and their actions do not represent the true teachings of Islam.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I felt a tinge of frustration as he pushed on further and asked why true Muslims were not explaining the correct teachings to these terrorists.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I must have sounded a tad bit annoyed as I sought to distinguish myself, my community and my religion from these extremists.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I told him I do not know these people, I do not understand their psyche and it was unfair to put the burden on Muslims alone to resolve this issue with regard to the terrorists.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the wake of news reports and the development of ISIS, I saw many Facebook postings of Muslim friends condemning the terrorist attacks but also expressing similar frustrations of having to explain to non-Muslim friends that the terrorist actions were not aligned with Islamic teachings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The frustrations soon turned into concern as we started seeing acts of violence against innocent Muslims all around the world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Islamaphobia was manifested in varying degrees and there was fear that the same would happen to Singaporean Muslims.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As the days passed and the terrorist attacks continued, it became apparent that anger and distrust against Muslims also grew.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Muslims also, in effect, became victims of the actions of the extremists who claim to fight in the name of the religion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I said in my speech during the Budget Debates last year that I have faith that, in general, the non-Muslim community in Singapore knows that Singaporean Muslims strongly reject terrorism and the misguided ISIS actions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Despite my initial frustrations of having to defend my religion and my community to fellow Singaporeans, I truly appreciate the fear and the stress that are aroused by the non-stop terrorist attacks in other places, especially now, as the influence of ISIS has come to our shores.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am worried about the attitudes that would develop against Muslims in Singapore, the impact on the practice of the religion and daily life.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I worry that the tudung-wearing Muslim woman will be discriminated against when she seeks employment.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I worry a Muslim is less trusted because of his faith.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The fear and the distrust are understandable, especially if you do not know anything about the religion and have not had any significant interaction with anyone who practices the faith.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We must continue to provide platforms for meaningful interaction among people of different races and religions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Our children must be taught to accept and embrace the diversity within our community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At the grassroots level, for example, it is not always easy to get representation from people of different races to participate in various activities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe some small changes can be and has been made.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Avoid prayer times or avoid the time slots when people go to church when you organise activities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Open up festivities to people of different races.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For example, invite Chinese and Malays to Deepavali celebrations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Improving the activities to meet the needs of the residents is always work-in-progress.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The education and training programmes, programmes to engage community to build capabilities to promote racial harmony as well as the resources – matters which Assoc Prof Daniel Goh had alluded to earlier – are actually things that we are already doing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We need to continue to do this and to work hard to create meaningful platforms for people to interact.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What is key is that we realise that we all play important parts in this work and we should continue to work together to build the bonds among us.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   Every day, we hear reports about terror attacks all over the world, who claim to fight in the name of religion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Their actions have, in fact, sullied the name of Islam.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should not just stand still and instead should try to correct the perceptions of others towards our religion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This does not mean having debates and organising lectures, but I think we can portray the beauty of Islam through our daily interactions and relations with those from other religions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We can do this at work, in school and by involving ourselves in social activities, for instance, at the CCs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many of us have already done so and I encourage more to join in this effort.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Recently, there have been concerns about some Muslims in this region who are thought to display extremist characteristics from the way they practise their religion.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This reminded me of the lessons I learnt in a religious class organised by PERGAS a few years ago.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I still remember Ustaz Hannan Hassan, who taught me at that time, and the knowledge he imparted had a significant impact on me.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is a religion that is appropriate at any place and time.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should adapt our religious practices based on our situation and context.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Since Independence, building together a multiracial, multi-religious, multicultural and inclusive society has always been the foundation of Singapore's nation-building.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Founding Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew stated clearly in the declaration of Independence what is the foundation of Singapore. "This is not a Malay nation, this is not a Chinese nation, this is not an Indian nation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Everyone will his place: equal; language, culture, religion." Singapore is a multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every race has its own language, culture, religion and values.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All the races form a big family called Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We can all see the efforts over the years to build a Singapore for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To build a Singapore for Singaporeans is the responsibility of every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every race must tolerate one another, develop consensus while accommodating differences, leverage different strengths and allow a hundred flowers to bloom.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Using English as the common communication medium is not because of its superiority but because it is convenient, used widely and practical.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the Founding Prime Minister had said, English is something that no particular race enjoys an advantage, hence all the races can communicate equally.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: People say we are like a rojak, but we are a plate of healthy, delicious and popular rojak.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think the Health Promotion Board (HPB) can use this as our slogan for Healthy Food Choice.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The IRCC in my constituency plays a very important role.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has helped many residents to resolve their misunderstandings and contributed greatly to racial harmony in the community.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In fact, in my constituency, there were some disputes involving residents of different races.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The consequence of these disputes can be big or small.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If they are not solved promptly, consequences can be severe.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I remember one afternoon at one void deck, a group of Malay residents were having a wedding ceremony.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At another corner, there happened to be a Chinese resident who was conducting a religious ritual with a puppet show.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The loud noise from the puppet show disturbed the Malay wedding.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Malay residents had mistaken the nearby Chinese ritual for a funeral, hence they showed tolerance and constraint.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, they hoped that the Chinese resident can lower the volume so that the wedding can go ahead.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I happened to be visiting the area so I helped them understand each other.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I was pleased to see that after some discussion, both parties demonstrated the spirit of mutual support and understanding.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The two ceremonies were able to proceed smoothly.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the end, they even congratulated each other.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of us would have encountered situations, such as frictions caused by neighbours burning joss paper.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through the IRCC, I have also helped two neighbours resolve a dispute caused by the Indian family burning incense.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just like my Parliamentary colleagues, I often organise various activities to bring residents together to build rapport and social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Among all these activities, I noticed that the durian party is a good one.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Different races can gather and enjoy durians together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The durian is not just a diplomatic tool.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Minister Ong just conducted Durian Diplomacy when he visited China recently.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The durian party is a good activity to bond residents.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The durian has become a common language, regardless of language, race and religion.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We cannot afford to be complacent, lose vigilance or take for granted our current achievements, stability and peace.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because if we are not careful, the mutual trust and tolerance we have built over the years can crumble overnight.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Only by working together can we prevent extremism from destroying our racial harmony and prevent the terrorists from taking any chance to undermine the peaceful co-existence of different races.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I suggest that the Government continue to strengthen national education, organise inter-religious, interracial exhibitions in various constituencies so that people can better understand one another's culture and customs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will also be a very good opportunity for new immigrants to understand Singapore's multicultural and multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Let us continue to build a caring, loving, supportive and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must stay united, regardless of race, language and religion to build a fair and just Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many constructive suggestions have been made, which my Ministry will study.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I also thank the Members from the Workers' Party, many of whom have made very constructive suggestions and we will look at them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will set out the types of threats we face, our response, and what the Government and the community can do.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, what are the types of terror threats that we face?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look at world and regional events − Marawi, Rakhine in Southeast Asia and, of course, the Middle East, these attract would-be fighters and others who feel angry.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look at the Southern Philippines, if the situation is not dealt with, it could become an operating base for fighters from the Middle East, who would go from this region and, eventually, they would then radiate out back into this region again, well-trained with fighting skills.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And that can take the problems in this region to a level very different from what it has been up to now.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This general situation has been made much worse by the mixing of politics and religion in this region and the rise of politicians and religious leaders who openly advocate intolerance.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, quite frankly, Sir, the direction, the trajectory of where this region is going is quite worrying.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And sometimes I wish we can be more frank and share with the people of Singapore what we know.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But both foreign policy considerations and security considerations make it very difficult to let everyone know what it is that we are facing.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is one type of threat: regional situation, world events.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second is the release of radicalised prisoners.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Laws in this region and some countries allow prisoners to be released even before they are de-radicalised.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are free to plot and are capable of inflicting harm.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The third type of threat that we face, of course, is self-radicalisation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Three Singaporeans have gone to the Middle East.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You saw one of them recently in the video.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There have been several calls for Singaporeans to copy attacks using vehicles, knives and day-to-day implements.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not say much about this, but it is there.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I do not know how many Members realised but, last year, we picked up someone who was intending to go off to the Middle East to fight.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was a driver of a large dump truck.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The fourth aspect of the problem is divisive preachings.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is an insidious threat which seeks to divide society along racial, religious lines and I will say more about it later.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the context of these threats, what is our response?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What are the operational responses to terror attacks?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, I do not intend to go into details.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There is a cost to be paid and that cost is imposed on us by the terrorists.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second is the community response, both to help prevent an attack and when an attack occurs, to deal with the aftermath.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The community must, first of all, be made aware of the threats, to the extent that we can make them aware of it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They have to be prepared, know how to protect themselves, and must be able to mobilise the rest of the community and protect the community as a whole.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And after an attack, we need to also mobilise people, make people come together to stand united.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our officers have knocked on more than 400,000 houses.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have spoken with 220,000 households, about one in two.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members of Parliament who do house visits will know that ratio.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have had 38 Emergency Preparedness Days around Singapore in different constituencies, 16 Crisis Response Exercises in neighbourhoods, and visited and spoken at more than 160 schools.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think the SGSecure team has done an outstanding amount of work, working with our partners − PA, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM), the Ministry of Communications and Information, the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth and the Ministry of Defence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But much more needs to be done and has to be done.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the context of speaking about communities, how do we deal with workplaces?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi spoke about this, the importance of ensuring that companies are ready.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have enhanced the bizSAFE framework to help businesses be prepared in the case of an attack.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are encouraging companies to develop contingency plans if their premises come under attack.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We use the Safety and Security Watch Groups.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is focused on the members and employees.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Last week, Deputy Prime Minister Teo launched the SGSecure Guide for Workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: MOM is taking an active role in this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Desmond Choo spoke about the importance and need for influencers to be part of the first responders when an attack happens.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: MHA and MCI are engaging high profile influencers to reach out to different segments of the community when an attack happens.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Next, we have to also consider building resilience in the community.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After an attack, society needs to pull itself together and stay united.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr de Souza called this "winning the psychological battle".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is the key part of SGSecure's work.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Several Members have made this point − a united community is a key factor in defeating terrorism.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you look at other countries, recent experience shows, once there is a terrorist attack, then there is heightened suspicion among communities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the current climate, that almost inevitably means Islamophobia.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If you try and strengthen trust after an attack, it is too late.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We need to strengthen cohesiveness and our unity now, do what we have been doing and add on to it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As Members have emphasised, this means going back to one of the fundamental principles of our society, which is multiracialism.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Let us recall what Mr Lee Kuan Yew said at Independence, "We are going to have a multiracial nation in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is not a Malay nation; this is not a Chinese nation; this is not an Indian nation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Everybody will have his place: equal; language, culture, religion." Moving, inspiring, determined.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is the Singapore we want, and that is the Singapore we must work for.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is useful to consider in context Dr Martin Luther King's famous "I have a dream" speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That speech, as many Members might know, was made in 1963, two years before Mr Lee spoke, but I think we can save it in the same timeframe.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: To quote a few key parts of that speech, Dr King said, "I have a dream that my four children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the colour of their skin but by the content of their character.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have a dream that one day little black boys and black girls will be able to join hands with little white boys and white girls and walk together as sisters and brothers." Dr King said this in America where a Judge had said, in 1965, "Almighty God created the races White, Black, Yellow, Malay and Red, and he placed them on separate continents...

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The fact that he had separated the races shows that he did not intend them to mix." This was from a Judge in 1965.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Dr King's America of 1963, he had to speak what he spoke about as a dream.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Lee, in Singapore in 1965, spoke in determined tones as to what Singapore will be.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was a vision for which we were thrown out of the Federation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Fifty years later, it has become more of a reality.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a reality we have worked for these 50 years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not a perfect reality, but we are on the right path.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is worth recalling this history, as we note the troubled race relations across the world.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not in Singapore have movements titled, "Black Lives Matter" or counter movements "Blue Lives Matter".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Terrorism, radicalisation, extremism, these challenges have to be met with the same dedication and resolve by us affirming the fundamental principle − multiracialism.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Murali Pillai made some good points on this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We often hear this suggestion: why do we even need to talk about race?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Can we not just say we are all Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Or as the late Mr Rajaratnam said: let us have a homogenous Singaporean race.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will make three points in this context.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, what is behind the ideal, the desire to do away with racial identity and create a single identity?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, what is the reality of racial identities today?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And third, how can we deal with them?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, this idea of trying to do away with our individual racial identities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, Du Bois said, and I quote: "he who ignores or seeks to override the race idea in human history ignores and overrides the central thought of all history." Mr Rajaratnam would, of course, have been aware of this when he formed his own views.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Looking at current trends, the kind of centrifugal forces that society is facing, including Singapore, online, there are different pulls and pushes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think many will agree it is going to be challenging to achieve a homogenous race of Singaporeans in the near term.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What we can realistically achieve is a strong national identity, a Singaporean identity, which will overlay our separate racial, religious identities, and that framework can create a vibrant society.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, what is the reality of race relationships today?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I quote: "The emotions between the races could never be pure… whether we sort out our demons or salvation, the other race would always remain just that: menacing, alien and apart." I quote this to show that even in a country that is often held out as the model of democracy, this is how a successful African-American, a future President, saw race relationships at one point in time.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For us in Singapore, I think it is safe to say, we have generally moved quite far from seeing another race as "menacing, alien and apart." That is the measure of our success.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: How have race relationships changed in the US in the course of the Obama Presidency?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This was 100 days after President Obama's inauguration.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Of them, 59% of African-Americans, and 65% of white Americans thought race relationships were good.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The fault lines are difficult to deal with in many countries.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: How can we deal with racial and religious fault lines?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many examples: EIP, several Members have spoken about it, the building up of our neighbourhoods.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng raised the need to ensure that they have sufficient interaction in spaces in the new HDB estates.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our national school system, with English as the medium of instruction; National Service (NS).

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In fact, we are often accused of being too interventionist and too focused on race.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I do not think one can be too interventionist in this context.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is useful to say what is now being said in other parts of the world with regard to race relations and integration.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But this is what the Prime Minister had to say: "…our country needs to come together to take out this extremism; and we need to live our lives not in a series of separated, segregated communities, but as one truly United Kingdom." Has Britain gotten it right, the balance?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In May 2017, she said: "There is … a role for government to help people and build up organisations in society to promote and defend Britain's values and stand up to the extremists who want to undermine our values and impose their twisted beliefs onto the rest of us." We go to Germany, Chancellor Angela Merkel said: German attempts to create a multicultural society had, I quote, "utterly failed".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Since the 1960s, many Turkish citizens moved to Germany for work.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The assumption was that the new immigrants settling in Germany would, over time, naturally assimilate themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But what, in fact, happened was the creation of parallel, isolated societies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The German government is now playing a more interventionist role.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have been fortunate that 50 years ago, our leaders had the foresight to deal with this problem without being clouded by ideology.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And their ideology was, "we want everybody to be together", which is a noble ideology.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Other countries' experience reminds us that we have to continue to build on the strong foundations that our country has had.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I am usually careful of such studies and reports.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They have ranked us sometimes at the top and sometimes at the bottom.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You need to check the methodology and the people who do these reports.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, if I could digress and make a point here: take the Reporters sans frontières' (RSF's) Reporters without Borders' ranking on press freedom.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have spoken about this before in 2009.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2008, RSF ranked us 144 out of 173 countries, below Guinea, Sudan, Pakistan, amongst others.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Thus, I pointed out in 2009, that at about the same time RSF came out with their report, the International Herald Tribune (IHT) had a news story on Guinea, in fact, it was one or two days before I made my speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And IHT said that people were being gunned down by a "brutal military junta"; women were being raped on the streets.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But in RSF's eyes, their press freedom was higher than ours.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And RSF, of course, continues to rank us poorly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I would invite RSF to please go there.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we have to be discerning about these rankings and how they are done and what are the political objectives behind them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And sometimes, ignore them, when they are patently false and not hold them up as a mantra.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: With that, I will say, we should be doing quite well in comparison with many other countries when it comes to religious diversity and guaranteeing religious minorities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And really, you do not need studies and reports.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Your experience, my experience, the experience of our people.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We can agree on the whole that we are going in the right direction.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think Mr Pritam Singh used that phrase in a similar context in his speech.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh said that there is scope to improve our appreciation of other religious groups.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many Members − Ms Sun Xueling, Dr Tan Wu Meng, Mr Liang Eng Hwa and others, spoke about the importance of each one of us as individuals, doing our part.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Sun Xueling called for all Singaporeans to take a small step forward, so that the distance among the races narrow.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They need to understand one another better; not drift apart and withdraw into our own racial and religious communities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Alex Yam said racial and religious harmony must go beyond tokenism.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We need genuine acceptance, we need genuine respect, and to honour one another.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is important that every citizen feels part of this society and has a strong sense of belonging.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We need to create common spaces, bring people together, facilitate interactions and build strong, meaningful relationships.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In this context, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh made some remarks on self-help groups.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I served as President of SINDA for I think five or six years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The ideal is, of course, that self-help groups should not exist and we should have race-neutral help groups.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The reality: CDAC, MENDAKI, SINDA, Eurasian Association, they are able to mobilise more volunteers from the respective individual communities, get more support that way.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As SINDA President, I told SINDA, let us get more non-Indian volunteers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we went out on a recruitment drive.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have some goals and ideals, but we also need to be realistic and practical, and mobilise the community along the different lines that mobilisation is possible and, at the same time, keep reminding ourselves that while we mobilise the community to help those who are less well-performing, we also remind them that they are Singaporeans and they should help everybody else.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And then, the self-help groups moved, provided tuition support for those of other races.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They opened their doors after having started helping their own.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And, of course, most of the load then goes on to CDAC because they have the most centres.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, again, it is something where the anchorage, the majority community, voluntarily takes on a greater share of the burden.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is not easy to achieve in most places.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What Assoc Prof Daniel Goh spoke about, the approaches are already happening.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Basically, the self-help groups and communal bodies are not mutually exclusive to fostering integration, if properly managed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The education programmes that Assoc Prof Goh spoke about, they already exist.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I am sure Dr Janil Puthucheary, who heads up OnePeople.sg, would be happy to give the Member a briefing, so that he will have a better understanding of what they do.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What we need is a greater understanding of what we already do in many areas.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Leon Perera acknowledged that we are not a fully race-blind society.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Other surveys show that there is a line among the races.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we might as well acknowledge that and then try and build bonds and a common identity.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Member made a number of other points about, for example, playing in common corridors.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That, as I have mentioned earlier, was a deliberate Government policy of building HDB estates in a way which integrates people.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Member also made a number of general statements, as I listened, and they seem to be almost everything that we are already doing.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, have some controls on speech relating to race and religion and, at the same time, also create some space for talking about them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Indeed, I would be happy if Members see it that way.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the Member said repression is not an answer.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I can assure the Member and everybody else, like he quoted, Saddam Hussein is not a model for this Government.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In Iraq, what you had was a minority suppressing the majority in the first place, quite brutally, and, now, what is being suggested is that the minority is being oppressed.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Neither is Marshal Tito a model for us.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our model is the governance that Mr Lee Kuan Yew, Dr Goh Keng Swee, Mr S Rajaratnam and others provided.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is the model that we have taken.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And that model, for example, allowed the Member, a person from a minority community to go from an HDB flat, playing with other races − a deliberate Government policy − to top schools and then to Oxford.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I believe the state paid for most of that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, in a sense, Mr Leon Perera symbolises the success of Singapore's multiracial approach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, I agree with all the broad concepts from the general points that the Member has made.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You have to build the integrated communities in HDB estates.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: You have to make sure your schools are open for all races.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The hallmark of our predecessors was to take the general ideas and then successfully convert them into practical steps.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And if we want to change any of that, let us have a care.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Member said we need to focus on the day-to-day.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, let us not forget that symbolism and seats of power matter.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, if every Cabinet Minister and every Member of this House were from one race, I think it will be a very different matter, would it not?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the Member accepts that, because he accepted that multiracialism is necessary in the corridors of power as well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As for the point that the cure must not be worse than the disease, again, I accept that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But also remember there are some aspects of the disease that look pretty terrible, like Iraq, like the massacres in the former Yugoslavia, like Syria.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We need to convert those aspirations into practical realities in a way which is doable in the context of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam spoke about the Muslim-only launderette in Johor.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Narrow-mindedness in the name of Islam seeks to drive a wedge between Muslims and non-Muslims.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We would not want something like that in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The tendencies and the risks are there and we need to guard against them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I agree with some of the points made in this context by Mr Pritam Singh and Mr Muhamad Faisal Abdul Manap.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Pritam Singh said neighbours willing to be open-minded, live-and-let-live attitude.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And Mr Muhamad Faisal Manap talked about open-mindedness, respecting the differences of people and national values.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This religious leader was originally from India, he is in Zimbabwe.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He used to come to Singapore regularly to preach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because we cannot allow this sort of preaching to take hold in Singapore and gain followers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Taken to extremes, such preaching can have very serious consequences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to be careful about foreign preachers who may not understand our context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I agree with Mr Muhamad Faisal Manap that religious teachings must be aligned with our national values.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our religious bodies do draw on religious leadership from abroad.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, MUIS has a Distinguished Visitors' Programme.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many distinguished Islamic scholars come and share their experiences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is important to be clear on the practices which will not work here and we have to be careful that we do not import the religious conflicts from other countries, even as we sympathise and offer help, where appropriate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh said our first loyalty should always remain to Singapore even if our common sense of humanity makes us feel for the plight of others in conflicts overseas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to be careful not to import those religious conflicts here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Alex Yam, Ms Sun Xueling and other Members have said our Muslim community has taken the lead.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have put in place a code of ethics for religious teachers and, on the ground, Ms Rahayu Mahzam shared that members of the Muslim community actively speak out against extremist preachings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That reaffirms that Singapore Muslims object to the misguided teachings of ISIS.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our National Council of Churches has spoken up against undesirable practices of foreign Christian preachers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The National Council of Churches came out after that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those two preachers had been contacted by churches in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They were coming to speak, we said no.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the National Council of Churches came out and told all churches to be careful whom they invite.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do need to really look at our practices.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to draw a clear line between what is acceptable and what is not acceptable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to develop our own style in the practice of religion, situated within the context of our multi-religious, multiracial society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mixing of religion and politics is another dangerous area and we need to guard against that because that is happening quite a bit around the region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is Dr Zakir Naik, who will not come to Singapore, but you can assume that Mufti Menk and Dr Naik are all around the region preaching.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many people go and buy them, including Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But such is what is happening and they are feted and welcomed for their viewpoints.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can have a sense of what is happening in this region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A religious leader telling people they cannot vote for someone of another religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Singaporeans will say that is not acceptable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if we allowed that kind of teaching in Singapore, you can easily imagine what else might be said by people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you are one race, you should vote for a person of that race.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a broad canvas of the kind of problems we face, some of the challenges, the approaches we take.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In concrete terms, what are we looking at in this context?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, let me talk about restrictions on foreign preachers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As such an open society, we cannot avoid being influenced by external developments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Social media emboldens some people to say terrible and evil things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Dr Intan Mokhtar spoke on the importance of community actors − parents, spouses, teachers and youths − playing their part in identifying whether someone close to them is showing signs of radicalisation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were constructive suggestions on how we can support these people to help.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister Dr Yaacob Ibrahim has highlighted some of the current initiatives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will study those suggestions and see how we can support them further.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our religious groups and leaders are generally very supportive of our efforts to build and maintain religious harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They know how important it is that our religions co-exist harmoniously and why we need to maintain our common spaces.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think everyone would agree that we have not arrived, and one never knows whether there is such a thing as having arrived.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore's approach, as I have sketched out, is to build a Singapore identity that can accommodate diversity and celebrate our different racial and religious identities whilst at the same time creating a broad common space that we all share as Singaporeans and can build our sense of solidarity as one nation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has to be continuously adjusted and refined as circumstances evolve, both locally and internationally.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In that context, the stronger religiosity that we have been experiencing across all religions is a source of strength, as long as we get the framework right.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we have to pay close attention to this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Almost 15 years ago, I spoke in this House during the debate on the White Paper following the JI arrests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I shared my view that it is an ideological battle that has to be won, and it is incumbent on all of us, as Singaporeans, to first reach across racial lines to build stronger ties across communities, ties that bind us more closely.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is the only way to cut terrorism from its base.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to win the fight for hearts and minds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said then that each of us must take a deep and honest look at ourselves, examine our attitudes, mindsets towards our Muslim brothers and sisters, and ask in our heart of hearts, do we respect and value them as Singaporeans, and accept them as equals?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or are we just being superficial and politically correct?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Are we showing them, with sincerity, that we genuinely want to build deep links?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That will define where our society is headed and that will determine whether we are able to come together as one people to celebrate the rich diversity amongst us and be the stronger for it or be divided by the differences and allow suspicion and negativity to tear our society apart.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I said that Muslim Singaporeans also have a duty to react in a way which will encourage closer ties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Freedom to practise a religion should not mean a total ban on the discussion of practices, which is similar to the point Mr Leon Perera made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That will hinder a healthy, economically productive life and active citizenry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It should allow us to discuss practices that impact on others in society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We must be prepared to debate this but handle it sensitively.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many of these points are still relevant 15 years later, today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will emphasise one of the points on terrorism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not tied to any one religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The man who killed more than 50 people and injured several hundreds yesterday in Las Vegas, as far as I know, is not a Muslim.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we have to be careful about linking, and I stand corrected, as this is what I heard Er Dr Lee saying —

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Maybe I should say, "I do not know".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That multiracialism can be discussed so openly by Members of many different races here in Singapore's Parliament is itself a strength not many parliaments around the world possess.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Furthermore, that we could achieve broad consensus in the debate that we have to stay united, regardless of race, in the face of a terror attack is itself important and positive.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We have agreed broadly not to point fingers at a certain race or religion, but to condemn in a single voice the abhorrent nature of terror attacks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: That agreement is not something to be belittled, especially when we see how so many countries around the world choose the fractious route of finger-pointing and ostracising.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, this bipartisan support for this Motion is good for Singapore and good for a united stand against terrorism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Alex Yam supported the idea that all Singaporeans have a role in being vigilant.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: He said that all of us need to be aware of the concerns, as well as the preparatory measures required.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Resilience after an attack is just as important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Desmond Choo shared the importance of having "first responders" online to initiate and shape discussions in a productive manner, as well as to dispel falsehoods and rumours.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Both vigilance and resilience require a collective effort.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In the same way, a collective counter-offence is required to diffuse the spread of violent extremist radical teachings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar has said, "  a shared responsibility,   which requires ... common effort and resolve." Yes, we have a range of laws to prevent the spread of radicalised teachings which promote violent extremism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: And as Mr Murali Pillai stated, it is important to have these laws in place now, before an attack occurs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But, as Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar also pointed out in her speech, more can be done upstream, well before muscular laws are applied.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar shared that she hoped that there will be more "social media savvy" asatizahs as they have a potential to be a positive influence to shape and influence the perception of the youths.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Google's subsidiary, Jigsaw, does it by providing links to credible counter-narrative videos.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These links are provided to those who had searched online for what Google's algorithms construed as potential terrorists.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The counter-narrative links are not openly counter-terrorist in name and title.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, as a result, that potential reader is not deterred.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In fact, what we are debating today in Parliament is also a counter-narrative to terrorism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: What we need to do more of is to put that counter-narrative into social media.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But we have not remained stagnant in that endeavour.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Our Home Team has worked hard to keep us ahead of the game.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: We have invested in technology and thought out of the box to keep ahead.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Importantly, we also need to guard against the deadly concoction of terrorism and drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Some militants were even found high on drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: This is not just a problem isolated to Marawi.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The Minister for Foreign Affairs of the Russian Federation stated at a Security Conference in December last year, "Terrorism is closely linked with the drug problem.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Illicit drug trafficking provides the bulk of terrorism's funding." Therefore, to prevent funding to terrorists, we need to make sure we do our part to stop drugs from travelling into and through Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: The third point is investing in multiracialism as the best socio-weapon to defeat the ills terrorism seeks to sow.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As Ms Sun Xueling shared, her aspiration is that Singapore will grow "closer to realising the ideals our nation aspires to".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam still retains the faith that the non-Muslim community in Singapore will know that Singapore Muslims strongly reject terrorism and the misguided ISIS actions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To that end, Mr Liang Eng Hwa stated that, "Government policies and laws alone will not be enough to bring us to that enduring level of trust and harmonious relations at the people-to-people level".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, for Mr Liang, people-to-people relations are important.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Leon Perera suggested to have more common spaces for people of different races to interact and integrate.
